10462-clarissa-harlowe-or-the-history-of:
Samuel Richardson's Clarissa Harlowe, in nine volumes, reaches its fourth volume here, told wholly in letters. Clarissa writes to her friend Miss Howe from lodgings she likes but little, under a widow she distrusts, while her suitor Lovelace presses marriage in ways she cannot accept. The letters show her caution over doors, windows, and seals.

Miss Howe urges daily letters, wonders at Lovelace's delays, and watches his studied tricks with women below stairs. Lovelace triumphs on small points and resolves to try Clarissa to the utmost. Readers get the tense middle of a great epistolary novel, full of moral struggle and social pressure.
10564-fairy-gold-ship-s-company-part-4:
W. W. Jacobs wrote short comic tales about sailors, lodgers, and working men in English port towns, and "Fairy Gold" is one story from his collection Ship's Company. Augustus Teak invites his old friend Alf Chase to lodge with him, and hints that his wife has a secret reason for wanting only honest people in the house. Teak then lets slip that she has saved a large sum of money and hidden it somewhere indoors.

The humor grows out of greed, gossip, and the gap between what the men guess and what they actually know. Chase listens with rising interest as Teak talks up the hidden savings, and Jacobs keeps the joke moving through sly talk in a pub and at home. Readers get a compact, funny tale of suspicion and scheming, told in the plain, salty speech of his Thames-side characters.
10784-sentence-deferred-sailor-s-knots-p:
W. W. Jacobs's "Sentence Deferred," the fourth tale in Sailors' Knots from 1909, opens with Captain Bligh tripping Police-Sergeant Pilbeam in a quiet street. Only an elderly man with a wooden leg sees it, and he joins the indignant officer in pursuit through the alley-ways of old Wood-hatch. Bligh's youth helps him at first, but the hunters multiply.

The tale turns on flight, hiding, and the law's slow comedy, as Bligh ducks into a brick-paved yard behind a flint wall. Jacobs keeps the chase funny rather than grim. Readers get a short comic adventure, complete on its own, from the author's riverside world.
10801-the-literary-remains-of-samuel-tay:
Henry Nelson Coleridge collected his uncle's unpublished writings as The Literary Remains of Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and this fourth volume, published by William Pickering in 1839, holds notes and an essay. Its contents include notes on Luther, St. Theresa, Baxter, Leighton, Sherlock, and other divines, closing with an essay on faith.

The notes show Coleridge reading theology with a poet's eye, questioning, praising, and arguing in the margins. Friends such as Southey and Gillman preserved the papers for the editor. Readers get Coleridge the thinker, wrestling with belief in short, sharp fragments.
10925-a-collection-of-old-english-plays-:
Editor A. H. Bullen closes his four-volume set of early English drama with this final book, published in the 1880s. Six of the sixteen plays across the whole set had never been printed before, and this volume adds Thomas Heywood's previously unpublished play, transcribed from a difficult manuscript in the British Museum. Bullen checked the transcript against the original line by line.

The plays come from the Jacobean stage, with period spelling kept in the texts. Readers meet plots of love, revenge, and mistaken identity, plus the swagger and wordplay of early modern theatre. For students of English drama, the volume matters because it rescued rare plays from manuscript and made them available to read and stage again.
11184-the-constable-s-move-captains-all-:
W. W. Jacobs wrote this short comic tale, The Constable's Move, fourth in the Captains All series. Mr. Bob Grummit sits in his kitchen, his wife's dinner getting cold, while she watches furniture carried into the house next door. He warns her she will be locked up for looking at policemen's furniture, since it is against the law.

Police-Constable Evans moves in with a walnut sideboard, bevelled glass back, and a piano, which Mrs. Evans plays with careless chords, to Mrs. Grummit's scorn: she has fingers like carrots. Grummit, furious that coppers get on and buy pianos, challenges Evans to come out in the road, but Evans replies it is against the rules. Jacobs's comedy pits a resentful neighbour against a serenely superior policeman.
11271-the-anti-slavery-examiner-part-1-o:
Published by the American Anti-Slavery Society in 1836, the first part of the Anti-Slavery Examiner gathers its opening numbers. An address to the people of the United States defends liberty of conscience, speech, and press against suppression, while Angelina Grimké's appeal addresses Christian women of the South directly. Gerrit Smith's letter to a Mississippi minister and a biblical inquiry against slavery follow.

A fifth number argues Congress's power over slavery in the District of Columbia. Together these tracts show abolitionist argument in its early organized form: constitutional, biblical, and moral at once. The volume is a primary source for the movement's rhetoric before the sectional crisis hardened into war.
11272-the-anti-slavery-examiner-part-2-o:
The second part of the Anti-Slavery Examiner, dated 1838, gathers numbers five through ten of the Society's series, with a revised power-of-Congress argument opening the volume. Beriah Green's chattel principle essay argues that the New Testament offers no refuge for American slavery, while the narrative of James Williams, an American slave, supplies firsthand testimony. Emancipation in the West Indies appears twice, with correspondence between Congressman Elmore and abolitionist James Birney.

Gerrit Smith's letter to Henry Clay closes the set. Together the tracts move from law to scripture to lived experience, the Society's three lines of attack. The volume shows abolitionism maturing from appeal to systematic case-building in the late 1830s.
11273-the-anti-slavery-examiner-part-3-o:
The third part of the Anti-Slavery Examiner centers on American Slavery As It Is, the 1839 testimony of a thousand witnesses compiled from slaveholders' own newspapers and statements. Its advertisement insists the facts rest on slaveholders' authority, with names and residences given as vouchers, and invites skeptics to read the source papers at the Society's Nassau Street office. A speech by Senator Thomas Morris answering Henry Clay accompanies it.

Selections from the Madison papers argue that the Constitution was a pro-slavery compact. The volume's method, documentation over denunciation, made it one of abolitionism's most effective tracts. Readers today find in it a grim archive of slavery's daily violence, assembled by its opponents from its defenders' words.
11274-the-anti-slavery-examiner-part-4-o:
The fourth part of the Anti-Slavery Examiner, dated 1839, closes the series with Beriah Green's New Testament argument against slavery. asking whether Jesus Christ favors American slavery and answering from Jefferson's 1776 declaration that all men are created equal. A companion tract reports on the condition of free people of color in the United States, while another asks whether abolitionists can vote or take office under the Constitution.

An address on the House of Representatives' violation of the right of petition completes the volume. These final numbers turn from persuading slaveholders to organizing free citizens: voting, office, and petition rights. The part shows a movement preparing for political action, not only moral witness.
11474-sam-s-ghost-deep-waters-part-4:
Jacobs's Deep Waters story Sam's Ghost finds the night-watchman thoughtful over a cold pipe, gazing across the river, answering skeptics who laugh at ghosts. let them take a night-watchman's job alone with water lapping and wind moaning, especially after a pal slipped overboard. Sam Bullet, a waterman who cadged drinks and left his tobacco box home, fell from a lighter, leaving only his cap. Two nights before he had knocked down an old man and bitten a policeman's finger.

Mates comfort his widow by suggesting Sam was taken for a wise purpose, happier where he was than doing six months. Sam's ghost, artful as in life, drives the comedy. The story shows Jacobs's ghost humor: spooky setting, mercenary spirit, and a punchline in dialect.
11954-a-popular-history-of-france-from-t:
Volume 4 of Guizot's History of France covers Francis I and his successors through the religious wars. Chapters treat Francis I and Charles V, Francis I and the Renaissance. Francis I and the Reformation, then Henry II from 1547 to 1559 and the brief reign of Francis II, July 1559 to December 1560.

Charles IX and the religious wars from 1560 to 1574 close the volume. Henry III and the religious wars from 1574 to 1589 follow, with steel engravings illustrating the court and its conflicts. Guizot presents the Renaissance, the Reformation, and civil war as a single crisis of French kingship, in which culture, faith, and power could no longer be separated.
11974-dialstone-lane-part-4:
Part 4 of W. W. Jacobs's Dialstone Lane opens with Mrs. Chalk watching a schooner until it is a mere white speck on the horizon, clinging to a faint idea that it might yet turn back for her. Forced at last to accept the inevitable, she rises crimson with wrath and denounces husbands in general and her own in particular.

Later chapters turn on the missing map and a harebrained voyage, as Prudence, wrathful, insists that Tredgold never believed in the treasure and can never come again. Sailors Brisket and Stobell provide the comedy's ballast, laughing over a man's queerness, while Jacobs keeps the treasure hunt, the marriages, and the seaside town in cheerful, tangled motion.
12124-the-well-the-lady-of-the-barge-and:
Set in an old country house, The Well is a grim short story from W. W. Jacobs collection The Lady of the Barge. Two men talk in a billiard room after play, and the conversation turns to marriage, money, and a crime one of them cannot confess.

Jem Benson, soon to marry Olive, hides a secret tied to a disused well on the grounds, while his cousin Wilfred Carr needles him about wealth and luck. When Olive drops her dead mother bracelet down the well, Benson panic gives him away. Jacobs, known for comedy, here writes a tight tale of guilt, where a small accident forces a buried past into the open. The ending is bleak, and deliberately so.
12154-the-weaker-vessel-night-watches-pa:
Half past six, no wife, and no tea: that outrage opens The Weaker Vessel, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Night Watches. Mr. Gribble, lord of his small front parlor for thirty years, finds the kitchen fire out and his midday meal untouched.

Mrs. Gribble returns late from a lawyer, bearing news that her uncle George, who made money in America, has left her two hundred pounds a year for life. Her husband joy turns to alarm when he learns the income stops at her death, and his wife, in tears, hopes he will go first. Jacobs turns a marriage of habit upside down with one legacy. The comedy lies in a bully husband suddenly dependent, and a meek wife suddenly holding the purse.
12204-bill-s-lapse-odd-craft-part-4:
Bill Burton, a giant of a sailor with a soft blue eye and a teetotal pledge, anchors Bill Lapse, a comic tale from W. W. Jacobs Odd Craft. The night watchman narrator praises Bill strength and good nature, then shows how both fail him.

Shipmates Sam Small, Ginger Dick, and Peter Russet share lodgings with Bill, who drinks lemonade while they drink beer. One night the lemonade gives way, and Bill falls into a long drinking bout that his friends try to cure with tricks, pledges, and a string tied round his finger. The humor is gentle: a strong man undone by his own kindness and by friends who love a prank. Jacobs keeps the dialect thick and the moral light.
12647-j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume:
Volume four of J. S. Le Fanu's ghostly tales gathers Chapelizod stories, The Drunkard's Dream, The Ghost and the Bone-setter, and The Mysterious Lodger. Le Fanu opens on Chapelizod with a joke. No ancient village that has seen better days lacks legends of terror, as surely as decayed cheese has mites or an old house has rats.

Goblins, he adds, though not amenable to police, affect her Majesty's subjects' comfort, and deserve statistical returns of numbers and activity. Tales that follow mix humour, dread and Irish local colour. The volume shows Le Fanu's range, from comic ghost story to chill, and it remains a favourite among his supernatural collections.
14033-plutarch-s-lives-volume-1-of-4:
Aubrey Stewart and George Long translated Plutarch's Lives for this 1894 edition, volume one of four. Stewart, fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, and Long, formerly fellow there, add notes and a life of Plutarch. A preface argues no apology is needed for a favourite author. Since the revival of classical learning, Plutarch has familiarised readers with antiquity's greatest figures.

Lives pair Greek and Roman statesmen, judging character through anecdote and action. A passage on a ruler who needed no election or popular votes shows Plutarch's political eye. The translation aims at clarity for general readers. The volume suits students of ancient history. It remains a readable Victorian Plutarch.
14114-plutarch-s-lives-volume-2-of-4:
Aubrey Stewart and George Long translated this second volume of Plutarch's Lives from the Greek, published by George Bell in 1899. Lives pair off in the classic pattern: Pelopidas with Marcellus, Aristides with Cato, Philopoemen with Titus Flamininus, Pyrrhus with Marius, Lysander with Sulla, and Kimon with Lucullus. Each pair ends in a comparison, weighing Greek against Roman virtue.

Anecdote keeps the history human. Cato's speech recalls Lucius, who ordered a condemned man's head struck off at a banquet to please a favorite, though Livy and Cicero dispute the details. Sulla's campaigns supply storm and fire, with rain flooding the Acropolis and the arsenal of Philo burning at Piraeus. Taxiles marches with vast forces while Archelaus hugs the sea. Students still meet antiquity here as character study: ambition, discipline, and luck judged life by life.
14129-the-works-of-charles-lamb-in-four-:
Volume four of Charles Lamb's works gathers his early tales, essays, and assumed-signature letters. Rosamund Gray leads, followed by recollections of Christ's Hospital, where Lamb schooled as a boy. Essays on Shakespeare's tragedies, on dramatists of his age, and on the church historian Fuller show his reading at its widest. A fine piece on Hogarth weighs the artist's genius with care.

Letters under pen names add mischief. A Londoner writes on burial societies and undertakers, on tailors' melancholy, and on the perils of being hanged. One famous passage traces Wycliffe's ashes from a brook into the Avon, the Severn, and the sea, as an emblem of doctrine spread worldwide. Lamb's voice stays intimate throughout: learned, funny, and fond of old books, old friends, and London streets.
14140-plutarch-s-lives-volume-3-of-4:
Volume three of Stewart and Long's Plutarch, published by George Bell in 1892, pairs Nikias with Crassus, Sertorius with Eumenes, Agesilaus with Pompeius, Alexander with Caesar, and Phokion with Cato the Younger. Comparisons close most pairs, weighing Greek and Roman lives side by side. Notes and a life of Plutarch frame the set for English readers.

Pompey and Caesar supply the drama. Romans hated Pompey's father Strabo so fiercely that they dragged his corpse from its bier, yet loved the son early, strongly, and through reverses. Caesar, reading Alexander's history, wept that Alexander ruled many nations young while he had done nothing of note. In Iberia he raised ten fresh cohorts, beat Calaici and Lusitani, and healed differences between states. Ambition, fortune, and character judge each life in turn.
15181-my-mother-s-rival-everyday-life-li:
Charlotte Braeme's melodrama, number four in the Everyday Life Library, opens with a question: what becomes of the children of great criminals who die on the scaffold? The narrator wonders whether kin raise them under new names, or whether the world ever points them out in later life. A recent English murder trial frames the puzzle.

From that grim opening, the novel builds a domestic tale of hidden pasts, rival mothers, and young people caught between love and disgrace. Braeme writes in the high Victorian style her readers loved, with secrets, trials, and moral tests. Fans of sensation fiction will find the book earnest, emotional, and full of plot turns.
1708-a-history-of-science-volume-4:
Henry Smith Williams continues his history with the modern chemical and biological sciences, moving from the age of Newton toward the laboratories of the nineteenth century. Experiments on bees and wasps sit beside major work in surgery and physiology, and the chapters show how chemistry and life science grew apart and then back together.

The volume's strength is its parade of workers and their methods, told in short chapters for readers without a laboratory background. Anyone who wants to know how modern biology and chemistry took shape will find the story laid out here in order. It came not in one breakthrough but in thousands of trials.
17377-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Volume four of Maupassant's works, copyright 1909, gathers The Old Maid and other stories. The title tale opens at Count Eustache d'Etchegorry's crumbling country house, where bottles fill at the pump, candles wait for dark, and ancestral portraits show a fallen house. Other tales include The Awakening, In the Spring, The Jennet, Rust, The Substitute, Allouma, and Simon's Papa.

Maupassant writes with his usual bite: poor nobles, lovers, soldiers, and peasants caught in desire and fate. The set balances comedy with bleak irony. Short story readers will find a strong volume, where each tale lands with a twist and leaves a sting behind.
17724-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-3-no-:
The Bay State Monthly, a Massachusetts magazine, issued this number as volume three, number four, in September 1885. Its opening piece profiles John D. Long, the thirty-second governor of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts under the constitution, whose wise and prudent administration reflected great credit on himself. Long was born in Buckfield, Maine, on October 27, 1838.

His father was a man of some prominence in the place, and the profile follows Long's rise. As a monthly number, the magazine mixes Massachusetts biography, history, and literature. Readers get a snapshot of Bay State letters in 1885, through a governor's life.
20158-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-4:
Lord Byron's works fill many volumes, and volume four holds poems from 1816 to 1823. Thirteen longer works date from June 1816 to October 1821. Eight short pieces come from the summer of 1816 alone. More short poems run from late 1816 to September 1823.

Those years cover Byron's exile, fame, and most daring verse tales. Readers meet the poet at full stretch, in love, rage, and wit. The volume's notes sort dates and settings for each piece with care. It suits readers who want Byron beyond the few most famed poems. Byron's exile years also produced Manfred, Don Juan's start, and many lyrics of lasting fame.
2094-the-writings-of-samuel-adams-volume:
Harry Alonzo Cushing edits the fourth volume of Samuel Adams's writings, covering 1778 to 1802, from the Revolution's middle years to the early republic. Letters open with military affairs, European politics, and the Articles of Confederation. Cushing's edition, published in the early twentieth century, remains the standard Adams collection.

Adams writes to Lee, Gates, Burgoyne, and others on prisoners, trade, the army, and the work of Congress. The volume is a key source for the patriot's mind, plain, urgent, and fixed on liberty and public duty. The letters of 1778 onward show Adams turning from rebel to statesman in a new republic.
2150-the-works-of-edgar-allan-poe-volume:
This fourth volume of Poe's works in the Raven Edition gathers his comic and satirical tales. They run from The Devil in the Belfry and Lionizing to The System of Doctor Tarr and Professor Fether. How to Write a Blackwood Article mocks horror fiction itself. Poe's comic tales, often overlooked, show a writer who could laugh at his own horror.

Later pieces include Metzengerstein, The Oblong Box, and dialogues on words, souls, and the afterlife, such as The Colloquy of Monos and Una. The volume shows Poe the humorist and thinker, not only the poet of dread. The Devil in the Belfry, with its Dutch town and clock, satirises order run mad.
2170-miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches:
Macaulay's fourth volume of miscellaneous writings gathers his speeches, dedicated to Henry, Marquess of Lansdowne. Macaulay prepared them reluctantly, suspending the history that was his life's work. Macaulay's speeches, collected late in life, cover reform, slavery, and India.

He feared reviving fierce old contentions in quiet times, yet the speeches show his oratory at full power, on reform, India, and liberty. The volume closes the miscellaneous set with the public voice of a great Victorian. His reluctance to publish them shows a man who prized history over oratory. India and reform speeches show Macaulay's range beyond the history he loved best.
22401-stories-by-american-authors-volume:
Stories by American Authors, volume four, appeared in 1884. Constance Fenimore Woolson leads the catalog record for this volume. Its opening story is set among Americans enjoying life in Rome.

The narrator had many acquaintances there, American and English both. No day passed without its invitation to go out. A literary man, he notes, is seldom good-tempered and well-dressed. Such a man, suitably provided with money, obeys all society's rules. When found, make a note of it, he jokes. The note was generally an invitation in his case. The volume gathers American short fiction of its decade for general readers.
22676-history-of-the-united-states-volum:
Elbert Benjamin Andrews wrote this History of the United States, whose fourth volume carries the story through the Civil War's last campaigns. The catalog record gives no year. Andrews, a historian and college president, wrote a full narrative from the earliest discovery of America to his own time.

The contents for this volume read like a drumbeat of 1864 and 1865: Missionary Ridge, Grant made lieutenant-general, Kenesaw Mountain, Sherman in Atlanta, then the March to the Sea. Columbia falls, Johnston is routed at Bentonville and surrenders, and Sherman stands master of the Carolinas. Chapter heads alone show the scale of the closing struggle. Andrews writes in the confident national manner of his day, and the volume still serves as a clear period narrative.
24360-the-life-of-napoleon-bonaparte-vol:
William Milligan Sloane, professor of history at Columbia University, wrote this life of Napoleon Bonaparte, published by the Century Company in New York in 1916, revised and enlarged with portraits. The first volume carries copyrights from 1894 to 1910. Its frontispiece shows Napoleon in 1785, aged sixteen, from a sketch by a comrade, once in the Museum of Sovereigns and now in the Louvre.

Chapters run from an introduction and the Bonapartes in Corsica through Napoleon's birth, childhood, and school days. Paris and Valence, private study and garrison life, and attempts at authorship lead to the Revolution in France. Buonaparte the Corsican Jacobin, the French Jacobin, a Jacobin hegira, The Supper of Beaucaire, and Toulon close the volume. Readers get a scholarly life of Napoleon's rise, volume by volume.
24941-the-nursery-october-1873-vol-xiv-n:
The October 1873 number of The Nursery, whose interior text calls it No. 2, continues the Boston monthly's mix of stories and verses for little readers. Threading the Needle follows Lucy and the maid Anna in a small domestic scene, while Our Pony and Nelly's Kitten keep the animal stories coming. The pieces stay short, sweet, and easy to read aloud.

Perils of the Sea supplies the excitement, as a boy wades into the water to save his toy ship, the Uncle George, from the waves. In Honor of Rosa's Birthday closes with a celebration for a two-year-old, a fitting end for a magazine aimed at the very young. The issue shows the nursery's formula working smoothly: home, pets, daring, and birthdays.
2622-the-home-book-of-verse-volume-4:
Burton Egbert Stevenson closes his Home Book of Verse with this fourth volume, again opening with poems of youth and age. Keats on the human seasons leads into verses for babies and children by Barr, Spofford, Blake, MacDonald, and Conkling.

The volume keeps the anthology's household spirit, favoring poems that can be read aloud and loved by all ages. Its arrangement repeats the set's pattern, so readers can dip in anywhere. The book completes a generous family library of verse, meant for shelves where poetry is lived with, not merely studied.
26317-buchanan-s-journal-of-man-may-1887:
Buchanan's Journal of Man for May 1887, volume one, number four, is a journal of psychometry, prophecy, and brain science. Its lead article treats the prophetic faculty through war and peace, claiming that psychometric prophecy foretold peace while generals promised war, then foretold war while statesmen hoped for peace. A Russian plan for Galicia gets a full hearing.

Other contents cover spiritual wonders, from Slater's tests and spirit pictures to slate writing and the fire test. A series on the structure and genesis of the brain runs beside notes on co-operation, inventors, artificial ivory, and paper pianos. The issue shows a Victorian fringe science in full voice, confident that mind can read the future.
2674-the-complete-writings-of-charles-du:
Charles Dudley Warner's fourth volume of complete writings opens with Being a Boy. That essay celebrates boyhood with a plain claim: one of the best things in the world to be is a boy. It needs no experience, Warner says, though it takes practice to be a good one.

On Horseback follows, with travel notes and rural scenes, and the volume keeps Warner's easy, humorous tone throughout. Boys yoking calves and playing at work give way to men with heavier loads. The book charms as a nostalgic look at American farm boyhood, written by a man who remembered it fondly.
27289-the-life-of-napoleon-bonaparte-vol:
William Milligan Sloane's The Life of Napoleon Bonaparte, volume three, revised and enlarged with portraits by the Century Company, carries the emperor from war with Russia to the retreat from Moscow. Sloane, professor of history at Columbia, opens with Pultusk, the check at Eylau, and the indecisive victory at Friedland.

Napoleon and Alexander meet at Tilsit, the new feudalism spreads, and Spain awakens in the first revolt of nations. The volume closes with Borodino, the evacuation of Moscow, and the horrors of the retreat, in Sloane's large scholarly biography of the Napoleonic empire.
28104-the-pulpit-of-the-reformation-nos-:
The Pulpit of the Reformation, numbers one to four, printed at Aberdeen in 1834 and 1835, reprints sermons from the age of reform. Number one gives John Welch on the Last Judgment and Bishop Hugh Latimer on the Day of Judgment. Number two adds Latimer on the parables of the householder and the tares, preached in 1553.

Numbers three and four add a sermon John Knox preached before Queen Mary, with part of his Admonition to England. George King published the set for readers who prized Reformation preaching. The sermons warn of judgement, urge repentance, and show the plain, urgent style of early Protestant pulpits.
2882-the-legends-of-the-jews-volume-4:
Louis Ginzberg compiled The Legends of the Jews, volume four, from rabbinic and folk sources, translated from the German manuscript. The volume covers Bible times and characters from Joshua to Esther. It includes the conquest of the land, the judges Deborah, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson, Samuel and Saul, and the long story of David. Solomon's temple building brings even demons into the workforce.

Ginzberg retells each life with legends that fill gaps left by the biblical text, such as a headless demon named Envy who delights in devouring heads. The result reads as both scholarship and storytelling, gathering scattered traditions into order. Readers use it as a treasury of Jewish legend and as a guide to how the Bible was imagined across centuries.
30991-the-esperantist-vol-1-no-4:
Held here is the February 1904 number of The Esperantist, the Esperanto gazette for spreading the international language, edited by H. Bolingbrooke Mudie and published by the London Esperanto Club at Outer Temple, London. Single copies sold for fourpence net, and the annual subscription was three shillings. Its contents show a young movement organizing itself in print.

Pages include the president's speech at the annual meeting, Dr. Zamenhof's greetings by phonograph, How to Found a Group by H. W. Clephan, a New Year's poem by Clarence Bicknell, a translation of The Tempest by A. Motteau, Zamenhof's views on an academy, and Giant Despair from Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, translated by Joseph Rhodes. Correspondence, science notes, and an Esperantists' hymn close the number. It is a lively snapshot of Esperanto in 1904.
31015-the-poetical-works-of-elizabeth-ba:
Held here is volume four of the poetical works of Elizabeth Barrett Browning, published by Smith, Elder and Company in 1890. Its contents open with poems including A Child's Grave at Florence, Catarina to Camoens, Life and Love, A Denial, Proof and Disproof, Question and Answer, Inclusions, and Insufficiency. They are followed by the Sonnets from the Portuguese. Casa Guidi Windows follows in two parts.

Poems Before Congress include Napoleon III in Italy, The Dance, A Tale of Villafranca, A Court Lady, An August Voice, Christmas Gifts, Italy and the World, and A Curse for a Nation. Last Poems include Little Mattie, A False Step, Void in Law, Lord Walter's Wife, Bianca among the Nightingales, My Kate, and A Song for the Ragged Schools of London. They continue with May's Love, Amy's Cruelty, My Heart and I, and The Best Thing in the World. It is a volume of Browning's verse.
31026-the-life-of-napoleon-bonaparte-vol:
William Milligan Sloane, professor of history at Columbia University, wrote this life of Napoleon Bonaparte. It is held here in volume two of a revised and enlarged edition with portraits, published by the Century Company in New York in 1916. Its copyright dates are 1894, 1895, 1896, and 1910. Its frontispiece shows General Bonaparte, drawn by Raffet and engraved by Langlois, from the collection of W. C. Crane.

Early chapters cover the rescue of the Directory, the Treaty of Campo Formio, Bonaparte and Talleyrand, and commotions in European politics. Later chapters follow the expedition to Egypt, the landing in Egypt, the disaster at Acre, Aboukir and the great desertion, and the return of the hero. It is a scholarly, well-illustrated volume of Sloane's classic biography, carrying Napoleon from Paris politics to Egypt and back.
31411-stories-pictures-tell-book-4:
Flora L. Carpenter's Stories Pictures Tell, book four, was published by Rand McNally and Company, with copyright in 1918 and this edition dated 1928. Carpenter was an instructor in drawing at Waite High School in Toledo, Ohio, and formerly supervisor of drawing in Bloomington, Illinois. She builds each lesson around a famous picture, illustrated with half tones from original photographs. September and October lessons take up Millet's "The Sower" and Landseer's "Highland Shepherd's Chief Mourner."

The book teaches children to look at art and to find stories in it, pairing picture study with reading and writing. Its method is simple: show the picture, tell its story, and let pupils respond. For readers of art education, it preserves an early twentieth-century classroom approach, where great paintings became the starting point for language lessons.
32616-the-galaxy-april-1877-vol-xxiii-ap:
This April 1877 number of The Galaxy, volume twenty-three, opens with a long essay on the Théâtre Français and its critic Francisque Sarcey. The writer admires Sarcey's series on the great Paris stage and sketches its leading players, from Regnier and Got to Sarah Bernhardt and Coquelin.

The rest of the number mixes fiction, travel, and comment in the magazine's usual manner. Readers meet nurses, exiles, and provincial folk, and essays that range from Paris playhouses to lonely outposts, giving a broad view of cultivated reading in 1877. The number rewards a slow read. Its mix of stage talk, fiction, and essay suits a fireside evening.
32983-harper-s-new-monthly-magazine-no-2:
Harper's New Monthly Magazine for March 1852 opens with a Franconia story by Jacob Abbott, then ranges widely: recollections of St. Petersburg, a love affair at Cranford, anecdotes of monkeys, a masked ball at Vienna, and a taste of Austrian jails. Mary Russell Mitford contributes personal sketches and reminiscences, and married poets Elizabeth Barrett Browning and Robert Browning get a joint notice. A story of Rembrandt and a piece on public executions in England sit nearby.

A monthly record of current events from the United States, Mexico, Great Britain, France, Austria, and Hungary closes the number, with an editor's table. The mix is typical of Harper's at mid-century: fiction, travel, biography, and news in one thick volume for general readers. It offers a vivid snapshot of what a well-read American household was reading in the spring of 1852.
3369-a-hazard-of-new-fortunes-volume-4:
William Dean Howells carries A Hazard of New Fortunes into its fourth part, not long after Lent. One day Fulkerson pitches Dryfoos an idea: a dinner marking Every Other Week's success. Dryfoos has stayed out of running the magazine entirely, yet Fulkerson can see he takes pride in his connection to it.

Fulkerson works from the belief that Dryfoos would gladly let that connection become public. On the days when the dinner scheme ripens, the novel's money plot and its social plot meet. Readers will enjoy Howells's irony: a proprietor who never interferes, celebrated for a success he never touched, at a dinner he never quite ordered.
33803-the-mysteries-of-paris-illustrated:
Volume four of Eugene Sue's Mysteries of Paris, in the Boston edition de luxe with etchings, picks up Rigolette's first sorrow. A will, a freshwater pirate, a mother and son, and a lodging house carry the plot through Paris streets and river scenes. The Comte de Saint-Remy, Doctor Griffon, and the sinister Chouette all play their parts.

Sue keeps his web of lost kin, false friends, and hidden crime tightening chapter by chapter. Etchings mark the abduction and other high points. Readers who have followed the earlier volumes find here the same mix of sentiment, suspense, and sharp social contrast.
33848-the-history-of-cuba-vol-4:
Willis Fletcher Johnson, honorary professor of the history of American foreign relations at New York University, writes the fourth volume of his History of Cuba. Born in Havana on January 28, 1853, and fallen in battle at Dos Rios on May 19, 1895, Martí was professor of literature, doctor of laws, and economist. He was also philosopher, essayist, journalist, poet, historian, statesman, and organizer of the final cause of Cuban freedom.

Martí suffered imprisonment in Spain and exile in Mexico, Guatemala, and the United States, doing his crowning work as head of the Cuban Junta in New York. Johnson's volume carries Cuban history through the war of independence that Martí organized, in the tradition of his earlier works on expansion and the Panama Canal. It suits readers seeking a detailed, early twentieth-century American history of Cuba's struggle.
3850-memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-mo:
Madame de Montespan's fourth book opens with a magistrate who served her well in the courts, President de Nesmond, upright and clear headed. At sixty five, long a widower, Nesmond falls passionately for Clorinde, a farmer's only daughter glimpsed in a garden below his windows, and marries her. His young wife, pleased with a fine name and title, does not love him, and a handsome Spaniard of the legation soon dances into her favor.

A second tale shows a foreign lady, Madame de Bleink-Elmeink, freed from her husband's violence by the king and begging leave to live in a French convent under his protection. Montespan tells both stories with her usual bite. Readers who like court memoirs will find this volume rich in marriage plots that end badly for someone.
3950-cinq-mars-volume-4:
Alfred de Vigny's fourth volume of Cinq Mars opens on a woman fleeing Richelieu. Madame de Chevreuse arrives with hair in great disorder falling to her feet, her chief beauty, and the young queen thinks the toilette less the result of chance than might be imagined. With sang froid the queen asks what has happened, and says her guest looks like a Magdalen in her youth, before she repented.

Madame de Chevreuse begs for rescue, certain Richelieu pursues her, and the sound of pistols, heard more distinctly, convinces the queen her terrors are not vain. The queen answers that if anyone here is to be harmed it is probably herself, and bids her come and dress her. Readers who like Vigny's court intrigue will find a volume of flight, fear, and a queen's cool courage.
3961-a-romance-of-youth-volume-4:
Francois Coppee's fourth volume of A Romance of Youth opens with a chapter titled Reparation. The late Monsieur Violette was not mistaken in supposing Monsieur Gaufre capable of disinheriting his family for his servant mistress, but Berenice lacked patience. The rough beard and cap of an irresistible sergeant major proved the girl's ruin.

One Sunday, while Gaufre recites vespers at Saint Sulpice, he finds for the first time in his life that he has forgotten his snuff box. The holy offices are unbearable to this hypocritical person unless broken by a good pinch of snuff. He leaves his church warden's stall before the final benediction and returns unexpectedly to the Rue Servandoni. Readers who like Coppee's Paris will find a volume of hypocrisy, temptation, and reckoning.
3966-cosmopolis-volume-4:
Paul Bourget's Rome novel reaches its fourth volume with the gap between Countess Steno and her daughter Alba laid bare. The mother is open, impulsive, and at ease with grand feeling, while Alba turns inward and guards her heart.

A scheming baron named Hafner draws attention to Alba's dreamy mood after the novelist Dorsenne leaves, and the household begins to sense trouble. Bourget follows the clash of two natures, one that expands with feeling and one that contracts under it. Readers see how love, money, and gossip pull a family apart in a city full of strangers who watch each other closely.
3979-fromont-and-risler-volume-4:
Alphonse Daudet's Paris novel reaches its fourth volume inside the house of Fromont, where a night of drama below and festivity above leaves Fromont Jeune in a sleep of total collapse. He wakes at broad daylight to face a business and a family in disarray.

A new employee enters the house as old ties strain and past choices come due. Daudet keeps the focus on work, money, and marriage, showing how one man's ruin touches clerks, kin, and friends. The volume carries the novel toward its reckoning, with the firm's fate and the characters' pride hanging on choices made long before.
3984-gerfaut-volume-4:
Charles de Bernard's novel reaches its fourth volume in a garden, where Christian slips away from his guests for fresh air after a trying evening. He feels oppressed by feelings he has held through hours of talk, and by a concealment that prudence made needful and honor made a duty.

The volume follows the cost of that long hiding, as stratagems and guarded words wear on even a strong man. Bernard closes the tale of love and honor with scenes that weigh truth against loyalty. Readers who have followed Gerfaut and Madame de Bergenheim to this point will find the endgame tense, grave, and carefully earned.
3989-conscience-volume-4:
Hector Malot's novel reaches its fourth volume with Saniel wishing that Phillis might never leave him, since calm comes to him only in her company. She is happy in her sorrow to see him draw nearer each day, yet she cannot give up the lessons that are her daily bread.

Phillis also cannot leave her mother alone, crushed as the older woman is by grief. Malot uses that bind to show how love, work, and duty pull against repair and pardon. The volume moves toward attempted amends, with the past still pressing on every kind act and every hope of peace.
3994-madame-chrysantheme-volume-4:
Pierre Loti's Japan novel reaches its fourth volume in the small hours, when lamps burn dim before household idols and Chrysantheme wakes in terror. She signs without speech that someone or something creeps near, and a midnight alarm breaks the quiet of the house.

The volume carries the officer's brief marriage toward its close, mixing night fear, temple feasts, and the routines of ship and shore. Loti's firsthand notes keep the scenes vivid, from dark rooms to harbor light. Readers sense the bond's set end drawing near, and the sadness that comes with a farewell fixed from the start.
4104-the-mayflower-and-her-log-july-15-1:
Azel Ames's Mayflower history reaches its fourth volume with the passengers themselves. The Speedwell's list gives the names of the Leyden members who, with the Merchant Adventurers, prepared to emigrate in the summer of 1620.

Ames admits that present knowledge cannot fix every passenger with certainty, and he weighs each name with scholarly caution. The volume turns a list into lives, tracing families, trades, and fates. Readers tracing Pilgrim roots or the human side of the voyage will find this the most personal volume. Each name opens a small, human story.
4260-andersonville-a-story-of-rebel-mili:
The fourth and final volume of John McElroy's Andersonville narrative turns to individual stories from the last months of prison life. Sergeant Leroy L. Key, who led the Regulators against the camp's Raiders and presided at the execution of six condemned men in July 1864, tells his own later adventures at the author's request.

Key sought parole from the camp commandant Wirz, worked in the cook-house, tried to escape, was recaptured and taken to Macon, escaped again, and was finally exchanged at Savannah. His account, set beside McElroy's own narrative, closes the book with a story of endurance and release, after the long record of hunger, sickness, and camp justice.
4404-the-shaving-of-shagpat-an-arabian-e:
George Meredith's Arabian entertainment reaches its later stages in this fourth volume, where Shibli Bagarag journeys with the Sword through an underground kingdom. From the Cave of Chrysolites the party passes halls of council, black pools, and crowded porticoes, guided only by the Sword's light. Veiled, statue-like shapes line the way.

The contents promise Koorookh, the veiled figure, the bosom of Noorna, the revival, the plot, and the dish of pomegranate grain. At a fountain, Shibli stirs the waters with the Sword, and a bird rises where the fountain stood. The volume moves toward the burning of the identical, the flashes of the blade, and the conclusion of the quest.
4409-the-ordeal-of-richard-feverel-volum:
Book Four of George Meredith's Ordeal of Richard Feverel opens with a reflection on beauty and its conquests. Beauty, Meredith notes, belongs to the hero, yet it works most lastingly on the dull commonplace man, dropping like celestial light into a slow brain. The April of lovers sets the book's mood.

The chapters tell how preparations for action were conducted under that April, how the last act of a comedy takes the place of the first, and how a breakfast is celebrated. The philosopher appears in person, a procession of cake follows, and the book ends nursing the devil. Richard's love affair gathers force, and his father's system strains.
4416-sandra-belloni-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Sandra Belloni opens at midnight, with Mr. Pole trying to revive old after-theatre carouses. He listens to Emilia singing while he sips a smoking mixture, his imagination eased by a chop. The quiet domestic scene hides the novel's tensions.

The book's chapters suggest that the comic mask has kinship with a skull, then follow small life at Brookfield, Georgiana Ford, and a first scourging of the fine shades. Later comes the double man in us, Besworth Lawn, the supper, and the defeat and flight of Mrs. Chump. Emilia's voice and Wilfrid's games drive the action.
4424-rhoda-fleming-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Rhoda Fleming opens with Robert and Major Waring in an open carriage, calling out Sedgett's name as a cab flies by. They fall back into their seats and smoke, keeping to a bargain that no harassing matter be spoken until nightfall. The quiet ride hides the novel's coming reckoning.

The book's chapters promise the expiation, the melting of the thousand, la question d'argent, Edward's return, and father and son. The night before, Edward meets his match, and Edward tries his eloquence, before a chapter bluntly titled Too Late. This volume brings Rhoda's story toward its hard-won close.
4430-evan-harrington-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Evan Harrington opens with a second despatch of the countess, which Meredith says advances little except to show the general's skill in mining. The countess, Evan's sister, wages her campaign for the family's gentility by letter, and her addiction to military science shapes her tactics.

The book's chapters bring a break-neck leap, the tribulations and tactics of the countess, and the daughters of the great Mel digesting him at dinner. A handkerchief, the countess making herself felt, and a stream flowing muddy and clear follow. Evan's secret, that he is a tailor's son, presses harder as the comedy sharpens.
4438-vittoria-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Vittoria opens with the opera of Camilla, where the heroine appears in a costume recalling a Titian portrait. An Italian audience, Meredith notes, judges a prima donna at first glance, comparing all they have heard with her appearance and manner. She is examined to discover defects before she sings.

The book's chapters follow the third act, Wilfrid coming forward, and the first hours of the flight. Adventures of Vittoria and Angelo follow, with a crossing of the mountains. Vittoria the singer becomes Vittoria the fugitive, as art and revolution meet in the opera house and on the road.
4447-the-adventures-of-harry-richmond-vo:
Book Four of George Meredith's Adventures of Harry Richmond opens on Harry's twenty-first birthday, with books and dreams like two rivers meeting. The chapters follow his meeting with the princess, a time on board a yacht, and a view of the Hohenzollern birthplace. The time of roses and Ottilia follow.

An evening with Dr. Julius von Karsteg, a summer storm and love, and Princess Ottilia's letter lead to an interview with Prince Ernest and a meeting with Prince Otto. Harry's German adventures mix romance with his father's grand parade. This volume gives the novel its most romantic stretch, among princes, princesses, and summer storms.
4456-beauchamp-s-career-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Beauchamp's Career opens with Mr. Blackburn Tuckham, some time after the events of the earlier books. Nevil Beauchamp's political fight continues, with a short sidelook at the election and a chapter touching a young lady's heart and intellect. Dr. Shrapnel's epistle to Commander Beauchamp follows.

Later chapters bring the baiting of Dr. Shrapnel, a chivalrous gentleman set in motion, and an effort to conquer Cecilia in Beauchamp's fashion. The first encounter at Steynham closes the book. Meredith's novel of principle in politics sharpens here, as Beauchamp's idealism meets canvassing, newspapers, and love.
4468-diana-of-the-crossways-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways opens with matter for subsequent explosion, then a dialogue round a portrait, with indications of the task for Diana. The political and domestic crisis approaches in company, with a little dinner and its aftertaste, and great political news with an intrusion of the love-god.

A giddy turn at the spectral crossways follows, with a mine sprung in a newspaper article. Darkly it is seen how the criminal's judge may be love's criminal, before the true heroine of romance comes finally to her time of triumph. This volume brings Diana's scandal, politics, and love to their sharpest point.
4474-one-of-our-conquerors-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's One of Our Conquerors opens with Nataly in action, as a ticket of herald news sets events moving. A conventional gentleman endeavors to examine a spectre of himself, and a small thing or a great one turns on the soul of the chief actor. Mrs. Marsett appears, and a shadow crosses a virgin's mind.

Later chapters lay the burden upon Nesta, show squires in a conqueror's service conquering themselves, and let temper kindle temper. A pair of wooers follows, with deeds unrelated and expositions of feelings, and old lamps lighting an abysmal darkness. Victor and Nataly's long irregular union faces its hardest trials.
4480-lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Lord Ormont and His Aminta opens with Lady Charlotte's triumph, on a day of sovereign splendor riding down the heavens. Gold-fringed shadows draw over plain, turf, blue water, and woods round Steignton, and a white mansion shines by an oblong lake holding the sun. Lady Charlotte shows Weyburn the place.

The book's chapters follow a scene on the road back, the pursuers, and the sign of the Jolly Cricketers. Under-currents in the minds of Lady Charlotte and Lord Ormont follow, with the first day of the contention of brother and sister, and the Ormont jewels. Family war and marriage strategy sharpen in this volume.
4486-the-amazing-marriage-volume-4:
Book Four of George Meredith's Amazing Marriage opens with Carinthia in Wales, in an August of gales and rains driving Atlantic air over the highlands. Her old father had taught her the rapture of smelling salt, throwing up his nostrils to sniff largely. Carinthia, the novel's strong heroine, carries his lessons into a hard marriage.

The book's chapters follow Rebecca Wythan, younger examples, and Carinthia putting one of her father's lessons into practice. A frightful debate, a survey of Welsh cavaliers escorting the Countess of Fleetwood to Kentish Esslemont, and changes discerned follow. Between Carinthia and her lord, and a dip into spring waters, close the book.
4693-famous-affinities-of-history-the-ro:
Lyndon Orr's Famous Affinities of History, The Romance of Devotion, appears here in its complete form, volumes one through four in one file. The contents run from Antony and Cleopatra, Abelard and Heloise, and Elizabeth and Leicester. They go on to Mary Queen of Scots and Bothwell, Christina and Monaldeschi, Charles the Second and Nell Gwyn, Maurice of Saxony and Adrienne Lecouvreur, and Prince Charles Edward Stuart.

Later volumes add Catharine and Potemkin, Marie Antoinette and Fersen, and Aaron Burr. They go on to George the Fourth and Mrs. Fitzherbert, Charlotte Corday and Adam Lux, and Napoleon and Marie Walewska. They go on to Pauline Bonaparte, Marie Louise and Neipperg, Houston's wives, and Lola Montez. Gambetta, Blessington, Byron, Madame de Stael, Marx, and Lassalle follow. Rachel, Swift, Shelley, the Carlyles, the Hugos, George Sand, Dickens, Balzac, and Reade close the set. Readers get the whole popular series in one place.
4919-the-letters-of-horace-walpole-earl-:
Horace Walpole's letters in this fourth volume cover 1770, written to friends such as Sir David Dalrymple with gossip, politics, and literary news. Walpole thanks Dalrymple for his History of Scottish Councils, attacks the House of Commons, and laments controversy as the curse of modern times.

Later letters follow Chatham's attempt to widen representation, Burke's and Savile's attacks on corruption, and the Wilkes affair with Parson Horne. Walpole's voice is witty, partisan, and endlessly observant. Readers get a front-row seat to Georgian politics, written by a man who knew everyone and spared almost no one.
5237-the-confessions-of-harry-lorrequer-:
Charles James Lever's Harry Lorrequer continues in this fourth volume, covering chapters twenty-four through twenty-eight. Harry crosses from Calais with his fair friends, meets a gendarme, stops at the inn at Chantraine, encounters Mr O'Leary, and spends two chapters in Paris, as his continental adventures gather pace.

The volume holds only this short stretch of Harry's confessions, bridging his Irish adventures and his later travels. Readers following the novel in order will find French inns, officials, and city life, all seen through a young soldier's comic and romantic eye.
5464-the-sisters-volume-4:
A paved road lined with sphinxes leads from the Greek temple of Serapis to the rock-cut tombs of Apis in this fourth volume of Georg Ebers's The Sisters. There the sacred Apis bull was worshipped after death, while in life it was cared for and prayed to in the temple of Ptah at Memphis. Ebers opens the volume with that sacred landscape.

The road and its temples set the scene for court and religious drama in ancient Memphis, where Greek and Egyptian customs meet. Ebers, an Egyptologist turned novelist, grounds the fiction in tombs, temples, and ritual. Readers get a richly atmospheric stretch of historical romance, full of sacred geography.
5470-joshua-volume-4:
A storm sweeping over the isthmus opens the fourth volume of Georg Ebers's Joshua. Waves dash high in the lakes, and the Red Sea, thrusting a snail-horn bay into the land from the south, is lashed to fury. Farther north, Pharaoh's army camps near the Migdol of the South, the strongest fort of the Etham line, as sand whirls in the gale.

The storm frames the Exodus story at its most dramatic, with an army, a frontier, and a sea in turmoil. Ebers builds the volume from landscape and military detail as much as from character. Readers get a biblical romance in its wildest weather, where nature itself seems to take part in the escape.
5811-following-the-equator-a-journey-aro:
Part four of Mark Twain's Following the Equator covers chapters thirty through thirty-eight, reaching New Zealand. Chapter thirty opens with a Pudd'nhead Wilson maxim about locusts and appetites, then records part of an afternoon and a night at sea before reaching Bluff early in the morning. Bluff sits at the bottom of the middle island, far south, nearly forty-seven degrees below the equator.

Readers get Twain in New Zealand, observing towns, people, and colonial life with his usual mix of humor and curiosity. The part treats Maori and settler encounters, landscapes, and local customs, never losing the traveler's eye for odd detail. It suits readers tracking Twain's world journey, and it offers a lively, opinionated portrait of New Zealand in the steamship era.
5821-the-gilded-age-part-4:
Part four of The Gilded Age, by Twain and Warner, covers chapters twenty-eight through thirty-six, and it opens with Harry's letter to the Colonel. Whatever Harry's language, the letter's news condenses or expands an episode from his visit to New York, where he called with official importance at a Wall Street address. A great gilt sign marked the headquarters of a company whose schemes drive the plot.

Readers follow Harry and the Colonel deeper into speculation, as New York finance and Washington lobbying intertwine. The part shows the novel's comic engine at work: grand plans, borrowed importance, and money that exists mostly on paper. It suits readers midway through the Gilded Age, where satire sharpens as the characters' fortunes rise and wobble.
5839-sketches-new-and-old-part-4:
Part four of Mark Twain's Sketches New and Old opens with The Secret Revealed, set at night in the grand old feudal castle of Klugenstein. The year 1222 draws to a close, a single light glimmers in the tallest tower, and a secret council meets there. The stern old lord of Klugenstein sits in a chair of state meditating, before speaking to his council with gravity.

Twain gives his mock-medieval comedy, where feudal grandeur meets modern jokes about secrecy and power. The part gathers further sketches in chapters that mix history, parody, and tall talk. It suits readers who enjoy Twain's historical burlesques, and fans of short pieces where a castle, a council, and a secret produce more laughter than dread.
5857-personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-vo:
Volume two, part four of Sheridan's Personal Memoirs covers chapters one through five, in the Shenandoah Valley campaign. Headings treat organizing scouts, Miss Rebecca Wright and her important information, a decision to move on Newtown, and a meeting with General Grant. Organization of the Union army, opening of the Battle of the Opequon, death of General Russell, and a successful cavalry charge follow.

Readers follow Sheridan's Valley campaign from scouting to victory, with loyal civilians and fallen generals marking the human cost. The memoir praises initiative, from Wright's intelligence to a cavalry charge that turned the battle. It suits Civil War readers seeking the Shenandoah in a commander's voice, with the Opequon as its centerpiece.
5863-personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-:
Part four of Grant's Personal Memoirs, volume two, covers chapters forty through fifty, from Chattanooga to the grand campaign. Headings treat a first meeting with Secretary Stanton, Rosecrans, command of the Military Division of the Mississippi, and Andrew Johnson's address. Assuming command at Chattanooga, opening a line of supplies, the Battle of Wauhatchie, and rebuilding the railroad follow.

Grant offers his account of the Chattanooga victory, the relief of Knoxville, headquarters moved to Nashville, and operations in Mississippi. Plans for the campaign, Sheridan's role, Butler's part, Sherman in Georgia, the siege of Atlanta, and the Army of the Potomac's grand movement close the part. It suits Civil War readers seeking the war's turning campaigns in Grant's own steady voice.
6177-pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-:
The Tall Master opens Parker's fourth volume, a story tossed about in mouths of Indians, half-breeds, and Hudson's Bay men, so travelers hear only apocryphal versions. Pretty Pierre, at Fort Luke when the battle occurred, sifted the business thoroughly before and after.

Pierre had a philosophical turn and never lied except to save another from danger, staying cool and impartial throughout. Though evil in reputation, he earned belief and trust. The Crimson Flag and The Flood in Pipi Valley complete the volume. The fourth set of tales alone is under discussion, and tales from the remaining sets stay outside it.
6189-northern-lights-volume-4:
A Man, a Famine, and a Heathen Boy opens Parker's fourth Northern Lights volume at Athabasca in the far north, beautiful in summer but cold and bare in winter. Chinook winds from the Pacific temper the frozen Rockies' fierceness, yet forty and fifty below zero stays cold after all.

July strawberries hardly repay seven months of ice and snow, however clear and blue the sky or sweet the short sun's journey. Some days the sun hides even without storm, behind fine white powdered frost. The Healing Springs, The Little Widow of Jansen, and Watching the Rise of Orion complete the volume.
6209-the-trail-of-the-sword-volume-4:
The fourth epoch of The Trail of the Sword opens with a brother's blood crying from the ground, as two men lean against a great gun aloft on Quebec's heights. October morning air flutters lace at their breasts and lifts the younger man's long brown hair from his shoulders.

His companion stands tall, alert, bronzed, and grey-headed, with eagle eye and glance of authority. He lays a hand on the younger man's shoulder and says he is glad Iberville has come, needing him and all his brave family, sparing not one. The younger man answers with honour and thanks for a governor present before Phips rounds Isle Orleans.
6227-the-seats-of-the-mighty-volume-4:
The Governor visits Moray in the chateau with a cold, grand courtesy, plainly meaning to make an example of his prisoner when the time is ripe. Moray almost pities a man so lost in his own office that he cannot see disaster coming. The chapters here climb the ramparts, meet La Jongleuse, name the lord of Kamaraska, and march with Wolfe at Montmorenci, ending on a sacred countersign.

Parker's fourth volume moves between prison talk and open war, with soldiers, priests, and frightened guards filling the night. Moray faces talk of witchcraft and strange sounds in the dark, and answers fear with prayer and steady nerve. It is the volume where the fortress world cracks open, and the war outside begins to decide what happens inside.
6233-the-battle-of-the-strong-a-romance-:
Detricand, a Royalist of the Vendee, sleeps boldly at the Golden Crown inn in Bercy, a town sworn to the Revolutionary Government and full of possible spies. He trusts the innkeeper, an old friend from fifteen years past, when his uncle held a small estate near the castle. In the parlour sit the landlord, two stout burghers, and Frange Pergot, porter of the castle, eager to spread word that an officer of the Vendee is in town.

This volume moves the story into France itself, where loyalty must hide under the rose and every stranger may be a watcher. Parker writes Bercy as a place of whispered Royalism, old friendship, and sudden danger. Detricand's boldness is the point: a man who will not skulk, even where a careless word could cost his life, and whose past keeps opening doors.
6240-the-lane-that-had-no-turning-volume:
Winter comes hard to Pontiac soon after the Rebellion, with little food, less money, and a parish that gave its barns and best cattle to the front. The village starves in silence rather than beg, living on sour milk, bread, and an occasional potato. This volume gathers eight tales of that hard time and after, from Medallion's whim and a prisoner to an upset price, a fragment of lives, and the tune McGilveray played.

Parker writes Pontiac as loyal to old France yet obedient to the English, proud even in want. The Cure, the Avocat, the little chemist, and Medallion gather over chess and cards, talking through trouble with music and wit. These stories honour endurance without preaching, showing a community that keeps its manners and its humour when its cupboards are bare.
6259-donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-eg:
Looking from a minaret, two figures take in Cairo whole, from the pyramids of Ghizeh and Sakkara to Helouan's wells, the Mokattam Hills, and the Khedive's palace at Abbasiyeh. Below them the city hums, with palm oases, rooftop gardens, and bazaars where women watch through small lattice panels. This final volume holds four tales: a young lion of Dedan, a man who would not be denied, the flower of the flock, and the light of other days.

Soldiers of the Berkshire Regiment climb steep slopes at Dihilbat, clear a summit, and drive Osman's men into mimosa bush with raking fire. Corporal Bagshot, keeper of diary and dictionary, reports the affair, and a popular man named Connor stands at its centre. Parker closes his Egyptian set with war, pride, and memory, as the city seen from above gives way to the ground where men fight and remember.
6278-the-money-master-volume-4:
Judge Carcasson's judgment proves true: a year after Zoe fled, Jean Jacques still carries Sebastian Dolores as a strangling weight around his throat. When a man has taken on too much, disorder travels along all the radii of his affairs until they shake loose from the hub of his control. Flour mill, saw mill, farms, store, lime kilns, lightning rod agency, cattle dealing, and money lending all pull at once.

This fourth epoch runs from misfortunes that come not singly to a greatest asset, an offer, a sleepless Spaniard, and a farewell that may come too late. A wind changes toward the saw mill, and Jean Jacques sets men with buckets on its roof to save it. Parker writes collapse as a chain, each link a business, a debt, or a kin tie, until the money master must learn what his empire was worth.
6963-elson-grammar-school-literature-boo:
William Elson and Christine Keck built this fourth book of grammar school literature for classroom reading in 1912. Part one gathers famous rides, selections from Shakespeare and other poets, and studies in rhythm. Paul Revere's ride, the charge of the Light Brigade at Balaklava, and John Gilpin's diverting history open the set. Browning's ride from Ghent to Aix joins them, with Herve Riel and the leap of Roushan Beg beside them.

Studies in rhythm add the Bugle Song, the Brook, the Song of the Chattahoochee, the Cataract of Lodore, the Bells, and Annabel Lee. Nature poems by Bryant, Hogg, and Shelley follow, giving pupils strong verse to hear and speak. The book aims to train taste and ear through the best known poems in English.
7013-journeys-through-bookland-vol-4:
Charles Sylvester's Journeys Through Bookland, volume four, applies a new plan for reading the world's best literature to children. The contents open with Father Ryan's Better Than Gold, Wordsworth's My Heart Leaps Up, and Whittier's Barefoot Boy. Kinney's Rain on the Roof, the Cid Campeador, Goldsmith's elegy on a mad dog, and Father Ryan's Mother's Way follow, with Tennyson's Song of the Brook.

A sketch of Longfellow by Grace Sellon, his Footsteps of Angels, and Lowell's lines to him close the opening set, while the village poems wait beyond. Sylvester, author of English and American Literature, chose pieces a child can love and a teacher can use. Only this fourth volume's selections are described here.
7136-the-great-conspiracy-volume-4:
Logan's fourth part of The Great Conspiracy opens at chapter fourteen, The Colored Contraband, with the first gun at Fort Sumter sounding slavery's funeral knell. Years before, competent authority had declared the general government held, among constitutional implications, power to emancipate slaves as a war measure. In starting the war, the South marched with open eyes toward that legitimate and logical result.

Patrick Henry, opposing Virginia's ratification, had warned slaveholders of implied powers. Among ten thousand Congress might assume, they might in war liberate every slave if they pleased, under power to provide for general defense and welfare. Only this fourth part's matter is traced here, as contraband slaves become soldiers and freemen in war's logic.
7157-the-prince-and-the-pauper-part-4:
Part four of Twain's Prince and the Pauper opens at chapter twelve, The Prince and His Deliverer, once Miles Hendon and the little prince clear the mob. They strike down back lanes and alleys toward the river, unobstructed until London Bridge, where they plough into the multitude again, Hendon gripping the prince's wrist fast. Tremendous news flies abroad, learned from a thousand voices at once: the king is dead.

Tidings strike a chill to the poor waif's heart and a shudder through his frame, as he grasps the greatness of his loss and fills with bitter grief. The grim tyrant, terror to others, had always been gentle with him, and tears spring to his eyes, blurring all objects. For an instant he feels the most forlorn, outcast, and forsaken of God's creatures, until another cry shakes the night: long live King Edward.
7196-the-adventures-of-tom-sawyer-part-4:
Part Four of Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer opens with Tom gloomy and desperate, sure that nobody loves him and that his kin have driven him to a life of crime. He tells himself they would be sorry only when they found what they had forced him to. He sobs at leaving school behind as the bell tinkles faintly down Meadow Lane.

The comedy of the scene lies in Tom's grand self-pity, which turns a scolding into a pirate's vow and a boy's sulk into high tragedy. Twain lets the reader hear both the hurt and the humour in Tom's vow, and the part carries that mood forward into the runaway scheme. This section holds Tom's dark resolve and his first steps away from home.
7245-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur:
Part Four opens at a royal banquet. A lady's fright melts once she judges the Yankee pacific and unresentful, and she grows importunate that he give an exhibition and kill somebody. The call to prayers interrupts her, and Twain pauses to note the nobility's deep, enthusiastic religion amid their tyranny, murder, rapacity, and moral rot.

Nothing, he writes, could divert these lords from the faithful pieties enjoined by the Church, and more than once he saw a noble fresh from cruelty turn at once to prayer. The satire bites through the banquet's glitter, pairing devotion with violence in one court. This part holds the feast and its pious, bloodied company.
734-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Edward Gibbon told the story of Gothic Italy in this fourth volume, with notes by H. H. Milman. It follows Theodoric the Ostrogoth from birth and first exploits to his invasion and conquest of Italy, and then his rule as king. The state of the West, its armies, and its civil government are set out in detail.

The volume also gives the senator Boethius, his fall, and the last acts and death of Theodoric. Gibbon treats the Goths not as mere destroyers but as rulers trying to hold Roman order. The book is a fine study of a kingdom caught between Rome's past and Europe's future, told with Gibbon's usual learning and poise.
7534-a-book-of-old-ballads-volume-4:
The fourth volume of Beverley Nichols's old ballads opens with a son's grim answer to his mother: Edward, Edward, what will you do with your towers and hall, so fair to see? He lets them stand till they fall down, for never more may he be there. King Leir and his three daughters, the source of Shakespeare's Lear, follows, with Hynd Horn and John Brown's Body.

Tipperary and the Bailiff's Daughter of Islington lighten the mood, before the Three Ravens, the Gaberlunzie Man, and the Wife of Usher's Well return to the uncanny. The Lye and Wilde's Ballad of Reading Gaol close the book, whose sources are listed in an appendix. Color plates show Hynd Horn, the Bailiff's Daughter, the Three Ravens, and the Wife of Usher's Well. It is a fitting close to Nichols's set.
7753-godolphin-volume-4:
Rome at evening finds Godolphin entering his palazzo in the fourth volume of Lytton's Godolphin, glimpsing a mantled figure in the dark that recalls Lucilla, then vanishing before he can be sure. Inside, papers and notes disappoint him, and he sinks into moody thought.

He wrote Lucilla the day before a long, kind outpouring, explaining his struggles and self-sacrifice, and owning that her confession first taught him his own heart. He promises help from her kin, and hopes his candor will console both her pride and her feeling. Love, doubt, and a letter left unread drive these chapters.
7760-falkland-book-4:
Mrs St John writes to Erasmus Falkland in Book Four of Lytton's Falkland, with better news at last. Emily is out of danger and may see him in a few days, for the last time. His forced visit, she says, harmed Emily's health and name, though her virtue still stands.

She calls Falkland fickle and wayward, the last man to make soft, open Emily happy. She sets aside rules of faith to speak plainly of the pair. The volume, told in letters, weighs a lover's charm against a wife's conscience, and ends a dangerous courtship with firm, sad judgment.
8169-gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrate:
Book four of Rabelais's Gargantua and Pantagruel continues the voyages and sayings of Pantagruel and his companions, in the English of Sir Thomas Urquhart and Peter Antony Motteux. As with book two, the text draws on Urquhart's 1653 translation and the Maitland Club edition. With Motteux's rendering of the later books and passages restored from the 1738 edition edited by Ozell. The fourth book, like its fellows, mixes travel tale with satire.

Pantagruel's sea voyage becomes a vehicle for Rabelais's attacks on monks, lawyers, and false learning, told through grotesque islands and comic encounters. The humour is broad, learned, and irreverent, and the translation keeps its Elizabethan flavour. For readers following the five books in order, this volume carries the great comic voyage toward its close.
8401-germany-from-the-earliest-period-vo:
Wolfgang Menzel's history of Germany reaches its fourth volume here, translated from the fourth German edition by Mrs. George Horrocks, with a supplementary chapter by Edgar Saltus. Volume 4 covers the rise of Prussia continued, opening with art and fashion under French influence, and moving through the later history of the German states.

Menzel, a critic and historian of the nineteenth century, wrote for general readers, and his history mixes politics, culture, and character sketches. This volume, part 21 of the work, suits readers following the long story of Germany's states toward unity, though it assumes the earlier volumes. It is a period history, written when Prussia's rise was still recent news.
8585-roughing-it-part-4:
Part 4 of Mark Twain's Roughing It, published in 1880, opens with chapter 31, where two men in the company cause Twain particular discomfort. One is a little Swede, about twenty-five, who knows only one song and sings it forever, and by day the party crowds into one small, stifling bar-room. No escaping his music, through profanity, whisky-guzzling, old sledge, and quarreling.

This section gives Twain's overland journey as comedy of discomfort, with fellow travelers as its chief trial. Readers get the West as a crowded stagecoach and bar-room, not as open prairie. Part 4 suits readers following Roughing It in order, and those who enjoy Twain's grumbling humor at full stretch.
8704-the-dore-bible-gallery-volume-4:
This fourth volume of Gustave Dore's Bible gallery follows Israel's kings and prophets through their most dramatic hours. Saul's death on Mount Gilboa opens the book, as the Philistines press Israel, slay Jonathan, and wound the king, who falls on his own sword rather than be abused by his enemies. Absalom's death and David's mourning over his son follow, then Solomon, his famous judgment, and the cedars cut for the Temple.

Prophets take the later pages: one slain by a lion, Elijah destroying the messengers of Ahaziah, Elijah rising in a chariot of fire, Jezebel's death, and Esther confounding Haman. Each passage stands beside Dore's engraving in the original, and the text alone still carries the scenes' force. Readers meet the monarchy's rise and trouble in short, memorable episodes, ideal for dipping in rather than reading straight through.
8724-the-three-cities-trilogy-rome-volum:
This fourth volume of Emile Zola's Rome, translated by Ernest A. Vizetelly, finds Abbe Pierre Froment anxious to begin his campaign in the Vatican world the very next day. Unsure whom to call on first in that intricate and conceited ecclesiastical world, he is lucky to meet Don Vigilio in the passage. The thin little secretary, with his saffron face, trembling fever, and exaggerated timid discretion, turns out to be well informed and mixed up in everything.

Through Vigilio and his like, Pierre learns how Rome's church politics really work: favours, fears, whispered advice, and doors that open only to the well introduced. Zola uses Pierre's quest for approval of his book to expose the machinery of the Curia. The volume deepens the novel's central conflict between a priest's sincere reforming hope and an institution built to absorb or defeat it.
8793-the-divine-comedy-by-dante-illustra:
This fourth part of Dante's Purgatory, in Cary's translation, covers cantos nineteen through twenty-five. Canto nineteen opens at the hour when the moon's cold beams outlast the day's heat. A dream woman appears to Dante with stammering lips, slanting eyes, distorted feet, maimed hands, and pale colour. His gaze, like sunshine on limbs numbed by cold, loosens her tongue and raises her form, until love's hue colours her faded face.

The dream of the Siren, and its unmasking, frames the terrace of the avaricious and the prodigal, then the gluttonous, whose wasted bodies teach Dante about desire. Later cantos discuss the soul's nature and the body after death, in Virgil's and Statius's learned talk. The part blends dream vision, moral teaching, and poetry, and it shows Purgatory at its most reflective, midway up the mountain toward dawn.
893-history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-t:
Gibbon's fourth volume opens on the Eastern emperors Zeno and Anastasius, then turns west to Theodoric the Ostrogoth. Born to a Gothic house, Theodoric rises through war and statecraft, invades Italy, and founds a Gothic kingdom there, ruling Romans and Goths together with Roman law and Gothic arms.

The volume weighs Theodoric's government, his court, and his fall, including the fate of the senator Boethius, put to death after a career of learning and service. Milman's notes aid the modern reader. It is a masterly study of a barbarian king who tried to save Roman order, and of why that order could not hold.
9167-the-three-cities-trilogy-paris-volu:
Émile Zola wrote Paris as the third book of his Three Cities trilogy, translated by Ernest Vizetelly. This volume holds Book Four. On a mild March morning, Pierre leaves his house at Neuilly to walk with Guillaume to Montmartre. Guillaume, gay and hopeful, plans to surprise his family after a long absence.

Pierre, by contrast, fears the lone hours that wait for him at home, where doubt and despair may return. The walk by the outer boulevards sets their moods side by side. The volume deepens Zola's portrait of a priest caught between old faith and new life.
9318-a-doctor-of-the-old-school-volume-4:
Ian Maclaren's Book Four, The Doctor's Last Journey, follows Dr. MacLure to his end. Drumtochty recalls the winter he lay two months with a broken leg, while the glen relied on the dubious Kildrummie doctor. Mrs. Macfayden claims a whup in the fifties, dismissed as a feat of memory. Forty winters of snow never drew a complaint from him.

Jamie Soutar tells how it took ten minutes to dig MacLure and his horse Jess from snow one night. The doctor never pled illness to any messenger. The volume is a fond farewell to a hero of humble service, and a classic of Scottish village life.
9446-samantha-among-the-brethren-volume-:
Boasting takes center stage in this fourth part of Marietta Holley's Samantha Among the Brethren. Folks tell a tale so often, Samantha notes, that they come to believe it themselves, boasting of riches or of past wickedness. Temperance lecturers and exhorters brag of how bad they had been, till the boast becomes their pride.

One man in particular made himself out an awful villain in evening meetings, worse than any pirate, yet Samantha doubted every word. Holley skewers humbug with Yankee shrewdness. The part remains a sharp, funny sermon on truth-telling and self-praise.
971-ethics-part-4:
Baruch Spinoza's Ethics continues in Part Four, of human bondage, or the strength of the emotions, translated by R. H. M. Elwes. Spinoza names bondage as man's infirmity in moderating and checking his emotions: when a man is prey to his emotions, he is not his own master, but lies at their mercy.

He shows how good and evil, virtue and vice, follow from our power to act by reason, and how reason can, with effort, guide desire.
