cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800290025-4:
Statement of significant OSA activities answers a request of 21 August 1964 from the Deputy Director for Science and Technology. The attachment describes the Office of Special Activities as formed to conceive, develop, produce, and operate covert photographic and electronic collection systems. Its staff is small: scientists and engineers working with support specialists and with industry, for speed and efficiency in the work assigned to the office.

Achievements named include the development of the U-2 and the A-12 aircraft. Praise from Dr. Edwin Land and Dr. James Killian is quoted on the office's design and sensing work. A later passage describes a project tracking objects drifting toward Soviet territory under a weather observation cover, which added knowledge of Soviet air defense deployment and capability.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02415a000800340029-4:
Draft history outline, undated in its legible pages, maps the OSA story in twenty-two chapters. Early chapters cover the Land Panel recommendation, presidential approval, a joint CIA and air force program, and funding from the Director's reserve with Bureau of the Budget review. Contracting chapters list airframe, engine, optics, cameras, and electronics, plus procurement for the air force and navy.

Detachment chapters follow, with build-up, training, deployment, and operations for each unit named. One detachment section runs from Middle East coverage in 1956 to 1958, through the May Day period and after. Closing chapters treat reorganizations from the autonomous AQUATONE project to OSA, intelligence gained from overhead reconnaissance between 1955 and 1962, and its effect on national policy.
cia-crest-cia-rdp33-02416a000300040001-4:
Briefing slides set out a new phased deployment concept effective 31 August 1967 for IDEALIST detachments. Phase I sends a forward detachment covertly to a crisis area as fast as possible, for a single mission. Phase II adds people and gear for three to five more missions if the situation requires. Phase III places a detachment where sustained operations will run for months.

Camera comparison charts follow, giving lens, aperture, scale, and swath figures for the B camera, Delta, and optical bar cameras at 70,000 feet. Detachment G duties at Edwards Air Force Base are listed: worldwide staging, flight testing of new gear, and pilot training. The file ends with the mission approval chain, from 303 Committee approval through alert, plan, and go or no-go messages.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200030005-4:
Office memorandum dated 1 May 1947 sends a redraft of travel procedure material for the CIG Administrative Manual. The sending chief notes insertions his office made: a section on temporary duty in the United States, an information for the traveler section, and added material under motor transportation. The Transportation Section chief is asked to review, correct, and return the draft.

The manual text follows the traveler through each step. Initiation, clearance, and approval come first, then the preliminary interview, travel order, clearance certificate, notice of departure, and confirmation of arrival. Rules cover advances of funds, granted on a bond of indemnity, and the traveler's duties on the road. Later pages treat vehicle accident investigation, storage and repair of official vehicles, and records of dispatch and service.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050058-4:
National Security Council order dated 1 December 1950 delegates a wide list of powers to the Deputy Director for Administration, CIA, and his assistant. The delegation is made by the council's Executive Secretary, under a council resolution approved 26 September 1947 and section 101 of Public Law 253. Personnel actions lead the list: appointment, termination, direction, and general administration of staff.

Allowances for civilian staff abroad and transfers between stations follow, with travel and shipment of household goods, cars, effects, and dependents covered. Other delegated powers reach tort claims under the Federal Tort Claims Act, execution of contracts, publication of notices, property rules for council staff, and certification of vouchers. Walter B. Smith, Director of Central Intelligence, concurs on the same date. The order takes effect the day it is signed.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050148-4:
National Security Council resolution, certified as approved on 26 September 1947, authorizes the council's Executive Secretary to control, supervise, and administer council funds. The powers match those a department head holds over his own funds, including the right to delegate. Delegation may run to staff of the Executive Secretary's office. It may also run to officials of the Central Intelligence Agency. Control of spending stays with the council throughout.

An order of 1 October 1947 then delegates in detail. Fourteen numbered powers cover personnel, allowances abroad, and transfers. Travel advances up to 1,000 dollars, emergency travel, and bonds of certifying officers are also covered. Some powers may also be used by the Chief, Budget and Finance Branch, or the Chief, Fiscal Division, CIA. The order takes effect 26 September 1947, with concurrence by the Director of Central Intelligence.
cia-crest-cia-rdp54-00177a000200050184-4:
Exchange of letters in August 1946 settles where the Central Intelligence Group's job classification sheets will be kept. The group's letter of 14 August 1946 argues that its work demands the utmost security. Classification sheets and documents on members' positions should therefore rest in a place with more than usual safeguards. Control over who may enter the area holding them is also required.

cicero-letters-shuckburgh-vol-4:
Murder and revenge close Cicero's correspondence in the fourth volume of Shuckburgh's 1899 version. Caesar falls on the Ides of March, and Antony rises in his place. Cicero thunders against him in the Philippics and pays with his life.

Private letters sit beside public fury in this most dramatic volume. Hope after the tyrant's death curdles into fresh terror and proscription lists. The Republic's last great voice is hunted down and silenced. Few ancient books end so darkly or so well, with the writer's own death as the final, grim proof of all he had warned against.
cinq-mars-volume-4:
Alfred de Vigny leaps two years forward in Cinq-Mars, Volume 4 of the English edition. His narrator borrows Shakespeare's privilege, he jokes, and jumps across time and space at will. Paris and the dark old palace of the Louvre come back into view. Two years, he warns, can change men and fortunes past knowing.

Cinq-Mars returns hardened, his favor curdled into open rivalry with Richelieu. The conspiracy that was talk in earlier volumes now gathers names, money, and foreign promises. De Thou still follows his friend, though dread grows with each secret meeting. Court ceremony hides the plotting like silk over a blade. Marie de Gonzague's marriage prospects shift the hero's hopes as politics shifts his plans. Readers feel the pace change here: youth and pageantry give way to whispers, couriers, and the first shape of a treaty that France will call treason when it surfaces.
conscience-volume-4:
Hector Malot lets success rot from inside in Conscience, Volume 4 of the English edition. Saniel, now an established doctor, finds his sleep broken after Madame Dammauville's death. Until then he had slept in tranquility, even after Caffie. Now he wakes suffocating and startled, with hallucinations crowding the dark.

Caffie, long effaced from memory, returns in dreams dragged back by the second dead woman. Long workdays fail to buy him hours of the sleep Shakespeare called sore labor's bath. Saniel diagnoses his own case with calm and private terror. Phillis and her brother Florentin's case press new choices on his success. Malot makes the haunting clinical: nerves, habit, and memory do the punishing. Readers in the final volume watch conscience collect its debt in the one currency the murderer cannot refuse, his rest.
cosmopolis-volume-4:
Paul Bourget closes his Roman novel in Cosmopolis, Volume 4 of the English edition. Count Boleslas Gorka lies wounded after his duel, beaten by the man he meant to punish. Dorsenne, the friend he struck at as a traitor, has humiliated him instead. His seconds, Cibo and Pietrapertosa, arrive from the Tor di Quinto races with careful, lying reports.

Madame Steno and her daughter were at the races, and Madame Maitland came triumphantly with her husband. The engagement of young Ardea to Fanny Hafner is public, and a cardinal has baptized the girl. Lydia Maitland's infamy stands discovered at last, yet she glitters on unpunished. Gorka counts his wrongs from his bed: rival, mistress, and false friend all happy in May sunshine. Bourget ends on that contrast rather than a tidy settling. Readers finishing Cosmopolis find its moral plain: modern society wounds faith and honor, then hurries smiling to the races.
curtius-history-greece-vol-4:
Athens crowns the fourth volume of Curtius's History of Greece, in Ward's 1868 version. Pericles leads, the Parthenon rises, and bold new thinkers question all things. Then the Peloponnesian War breaks out and shadows the glory.

Curtius writes the golden age with feeling for both its shine and its cost. Drama, sculpture, and debate flourish beside plague and ambition. Athens gains an empire and begins to lose its soul. The volume holds his history's brightest and saddest turn in one. A city stands at its height, already sowing the strife that would bring it down in time.
diana-of-the-crossways-volume-4:
The fourth volume of George Meredith's Diana of the Crossways covers chapters twenty-seven to thirty-five. Matter for a subsequent explosion is laid quietly in place. A dialogue around a portrait shows Diana as adviser to Percy Dacier, the young minister of state. Political and domestic crises approach in company.

A little dinner leaves an aftertaste of danger. Diana's enemies whisper that she sells political secrets, and the charge gathers force. Meredith darkly hints that the criminal's judge may be love's own appointee. The true heroine of romance comes at last to her time of trial. These chapters tighten the net around a woman whose wit made her famous and vulnerable. Talk itself becomes evidence against her, in a novel built from conversation.
dio-cassius-roman-history-cary-vol-4:
Books forty-one through forty-five of Dio Cassius cover the civil war of Caesar and Pompey and what came after. They appear here in Earnest Cary's Loeb English, the fourth volume of his set. Dio wrote around 230 CE, drawing on records and tales that have since been lost.

Caesar crosses the Rubicon, wins at Pharsalus, and takes sole power in Rome. Dio follows his reforms, his rule, and the daggers of the Ides of March. Speeches and omens fill out the story. No Roman writer gives a fuller run of these years, and Dio's books form the spine of the set's middle.
dionysius-halicarnassus-roman-antiquitie:
The fourth volume of Edward Spelman's 1758 English Dionysius holds books nine through eleven of the Roman Antiquities, with an index. Dionysius wrote around 7 BCE, and his huge history of early Rome ends, as far as it survives, in the early fourth century BCE.

These books give the decemvirs, the ten men whose rule turned harsh and shook the state, and the wars that followed. Dionysius wrote with a Greek reader in mind, keen to prove Rome Greek in its roots. His work stays our fullest source for the regal age and the early republic. Later books are lost past this point.
donovan-pasha-and-some-people-of-egypt-v:
Donovan Pasha and Some People of Egypt, Volume 4, by Gilbert Parker, opens above Cairo at Ramadan. In A Young Lion of Dedan, two men look out from a minaret. The Pyramids of Ghizeh and Sakkara stand far off. Nearer lie the tombs of the Caliphs and the Khedive's palace. Below them the city spreads its roof gardens and minarets. Housewives lounge on the housetops. Harem women watch through carved panels.

The two watchers are Dicky Donovan and Captain Renshaw of the American Consulate. Donovan is now English Secretary to the Khedive. Parker says no man in Egypt held more importance. It could neither be bought nor sold. He Would Not Be Denied, The Flower of the Flock, and The Light of Other Days complete this final volume. The cycle ends where it lived, between palace and bazaar, with reputation as the only real currency.
elson-grammar-school-literature-book-4:
William H. Elson and Christine Keck's Elson Grammar School Literature, Book Four, is a school reader for grammar-school pupils. Elson, superintendent of schools in Cleveland, joined with Keck, principal of the Sigsbee School in Grand Rapids, to assemble it.

The first part offers famous rides, from Longfellow's Paul Revere's Ride to Tennyson's Charge of the Light Brigade, with selections from Shakespeare and other poets and studies in rhythm. Later parts add nature poems, stories and patriotic pieces by Bryant, Shelley, Byron, Poe and others. Teachers and collectors of schoolbooks will find it a rich, old-fashioned anthology, built to teach reading through great verse.
ethics-part-4:
Benedict de Spinoza calls part four of his Ethics, in Elwes's translation, Of Human Bondage, or the Strength of the Emotions. His preface defines bondage plainly: a man prey to his emotions is not his own master and often follows the worse course while seeing the better. Perfection, good, and evil are first redefined as useful notions, not facts of nature.

The propositions show why reason counsels cooperation, honesty, and the state, whose laws settle by common consent what belongs to each man. Justice and sin, he notes, are ideas from outside, not attributes of the mind itself. Part four is Spinoza's ethics in the everyday sense: how people can live together with less fear.
euripides-plays-way-loeb-1912-vol-4:
The fourth Way volume of Euripides, first printed in 1912, holds Ion, Hippolytus, Medea, and Alcestis. The scan staged here is a 1928 reprint. Medea, the most famous of the four, gives the foreign wife who murders her own children to wound the husband who discarded her.

Hippolytus shows a queen's false charge destroying the stepson who scorned love. Alcestis opens the set's lighter side: a wife dies for her husband, and Heracles wrestles Death to bring her back. Ion traces a temple foundling to his royal, god-touched birth. With this volume Way's Loeb Euripides stands complete in nineteen plays. English readers gained the whole poet in verse at last.
evan-harrington-volume-4:
The fourth volume of George Meredith's Evan Harrington runs from chapter nineteen to chapter twenty-five. Letters from the Countess de Saldar, Evan's managing sister, drive much of this stretch. She reports a runaway wife sheltered by Lady Jocelyn and manoeuvres around the scandal. Her despatches mix high comedy with cool calculation.

A break-neck leap gives the volume its physical climax. The daughters of the great Mel must digest their father's memory at a grand dinner. Evan's double life, gentleman abroad and tailor's son at home, strains every relation. Rose Jocelyn's family watches him with growing suspicion. Meredith ends the portion with a stream flowing muddy and clear, an image for reputations in doubt. Courtship, family pride, and the fear of the shop counter fill these chapters.
fairy-gold-ship-s-company-part-4:
Jacobs's Fairy Gold is the fourth part of his Ship's Company story set. W. W. Jacobs wrote these comic tales of working men and sharp talk. This part opens in talk between Mr. Augustus Teak and his friend Mr. Chase. Teak presses Chase to come for a pint and talk things over.

Teak wants Chase as a lodger in his house of thirteen years' standing. His former lodger, Mr. Dunn, left the week before. Mrs. Teak insists on honest folk under her roof, for a reason she guards. Teak whispers that she is a rich woman, then breaks off. The bar of the Ship and Anchor frames the bargaining. Jacobs builds the humor from hint, greed, and wary friendship.
falkland-book-4:
Lytton's Falkland, Book 4 opens with a letter from Mrs. St. John to Erasmus Falkland. Edward Bulwer-Lytton's tale here speaks through a blunt family friend. Emily is out of danger at last, the letter reports. Her health and reputation suffered from Falkland's forced visit to her room.

Mrs. St. John hopes the next meeting will be the last. Emily's happiness is injured for life, though her virtue stands spared. The writer then answers Falkland's charge of bitterness head on. Emily is soft and susceptible, she says, while he is fickle and wayward. No change in him would pass unnoticed by such a wife. Book 4 judges the lover in plain terms seldom used to his face.
famous-affinities-of-history-the-romance:
Lyndon Orr's Famous Affinities of History, complete in four volumes, gathers thirty-two famous love stories. The set opens with Antony and Cleopatra, whom Orr calls the most remarkable lovers of nineteen centuries. Abelard and Heloise, Elizabeth and Leicester, and Mary Queen of Scots follow. Courts, camps, and battlefields supply the early settings.

Later volumes move through Catharine and Potemkin, Napoleon and Marie Walewska, and Aaron Burr. The wives of General Houston bring the survey to America. Writers dominate the final volume: Swift, Shelley, the Carlyles, Dickens, and Balzac. Orr's subtitle, The Romance of Devotion, states his measure throughout. He asks what each great figure gave up for love. The result is popular history as a gallery of grand attachments, readable and romantic rather than critical.
following-the-equator-a-journey-around-t:
Following the Equator, Part 4, by Mark Twain, lands in New Zealand at Bluff, at the bottom of the middle island. Twain notes that Bluff sits nearly forty seven degrees below the equator. That is as far south as Quebec lies north of it. Yet the climate refuses the comparison. Winters are moderate, summers are moderate, and the temperature difference between seasons stays remarkably small.

Chapter XXX then takes up the rabbit question. New Zealand's rabbit plague began at Bluff, Twain reports. The man who introduced the animal was banqueted. They would hang him now, he adds. Around that joke Twain builds a small essay on natural enemies and colonial introduction. Poachers check rabbits in England. In Bluff the work falls to imported stoats, weasels, ferrets, cats, and mongooses, none of them native. Travel writing becomes environmental history here.
freeman-norman-conquest-vol-4:
William's reign and the settlement of England fill the fourth volume of Freeman's Norman Conquest, from 1867. The Domesday survey counts every hide and plow team in the realm. A feudal order is imposed from above on a conquered people.

Freeman traces how conquest remade laws, language, and landholding for good. Norman lords take English acres, and a new England takes shape. His learning maps the change parish by parish, almost hide by hide. The volume turns from battle to the slower, deeper work of rule, showing how a kingdom is remade after the swords are sheathed.
fromont-and-risler-volume-4:
Alphonse Daudet brings his factory novel to its crisis in Fromont and Risler, Volume 4 of the English edition. Risler walks home through snow, dreaming of profits and the house's good name. Carriages line the street for Sidonie's ball, which she excused him from attending. He pauses to admire her shadow behind the curtains.

Another shadow tells the reader what the husband cannot see. Sidonie's treachery with Georges Fromont moves toward discovery in this volume. Risler's worship curdles as accounts and signs align against his happiness. Daudet stages the fall inside the world Risler built: ballroom, factory, and counting house under one roof. The honest Swiss engineer must choose between shame, revenge, and self-destruction. Readers closing the volumes get Daudet's saddest design: a good man's trust spent as fuel for two people's ruinous affair.
froude-history-england-vol-4:
Two short reigns tear England apart in the fourth volume of Froude's History, from 1858. Edward the Sixth, a boy king, backs a bold Protestant experiment. Mary then restores Rome's faith and burns heretics in her Catholic reaction.

Froude tells the religious seesaw with pace and strong feeling. Prayer books change, altars rise and fall, and subjects pay in blood. Each reign undoes the other's work within a few short years. The volume sets the stage for Elizabeth's settlement, showing a nation weary of swings in faith and hungry for a steady hand on the throne at last.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-4:
Joint Chiefs of Staff minutes for July 17, 1945, take up the military side of Japan's surrender formula. The top secret extracts are an unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two of the Potsdam papers. The paper before the chiefs had been drafted by the State, War, and Navy departments.

Admiral Leahy said the Joint Strategic Survey Committee backed that draft, with one change in its closing part. General Marshall then gave the military view in plain terms. Nothing should be done before fighting ends that would signal the Emperor's removal. His staying in office, Marshall argued, might sway the ending of hostilities in areas outside Japan itself. An Emperor's order could stop distant garrisons that no Allied force could quickly reach. The minutes catch the chiefs treating the throne as a tool for ending the war, not as a prize of it.
frus-1952-1954-american-republics-vol-4:
Volume four of Foreign Relations of the United States for 1952 to 1954 covers the American republics: United States policy toward Latin America in the early Eisenhower years. The Office of the Historian compiled it from declassified records. The Cold War had come to the hemisphere, and Washington read local reform as communist advance.

The volume's centerpiece is Guatemala: the documentary record of PBSUCCESS, the 1954 CIA operation that overthrew President Jacobo Arbenz. Around it stand the era's aid programs, arms deals, and anti-communist diplomacy across the region. The papers show how one covert success became a template used for a generation. The records are public government documents.
gao-gaoreports-b-293435-4:
The matter of Career Quest, a division of Syllan Careers, Inc., is decided in GAO file B-293435.4, dated March 31, 2005. Career Quest protested a General Services Administration cost study under Circular A-76. The study compared keeping help desk work in-house against contracting it out. The work served users of the Federal Supply Schedule. GAO denied the protest. The record showed that the agency's in-house plan, and the scoring of it, were sound. Both fit the work statement and the A-76 guidance.

The firm had argued that the study was run in ways that skewed the result. GAO found the flaws alleged were not borne out.
gao-gaoreports-b-294605-4:
Yang Enterprises, Inc., and Santa Barbara Applied Research, Inc., are the protesters in companion GAO files B-294605.4 through B-294605.6, dated April 1, 2005. The Air Force had awarded Call Henry, Inc., the launch operations support contract at Vandenberg Air Force Base. GAO denied the protests on each ground raised. The scoring of the winner's technical offer and past performance was sound. Talks with offerors gave them a fair chance to meet the agency's concerns.

A third point takes up price. Even where cost counts least, an agency may pick the cheaper, lower-rated offer. It must only judge fairly that the premium for the higher-rated offer is too great.
gao-gaoreports-b-294722-4:
GAO ruled in file B-294722.4 on July 28, 2005, in the protest brought by SGT, Inc. The Space and Naval Warfare Systems Command had awarded Systems Integration and Management, Inc., a support services contract at its New Orleans technology center. The work covered business, operations, and administrative support. SGT attacked the scoring of both its cost offer and its technical offer. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

Two short digest points carry the ruling. The agency's cost realism adjustments were fair. The record also supported its view of the technical offers. With both points held, the award stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-294974-4:
Envirosolve LLC's second fight with the Drug Enforcement Administration is decided in GAO file B-294974.4, dated June 8, 2005. The agency had set up blanket purchase agreements for hazardous waste cleanup services. Envirosolve's first protest was dismissed as academic when the agency promised corrective action. The firm then protested that the promised fix never came. GAO sustained the new protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

The record showed that the agency had failed to carry out its own promised remedy on points that were clearly meritorious. The firm had thus been put to the cost of protesting twice on the same ground.
gao-gaoreports-b-295126-4:
GAO file B-295126.4, dated June 14, 2007, names Engineered Electric Company, doing business as DRS Fermont, as the protester. The firm attacked the terms of an Army solicitation for tactical quiet generator sets and standard generator sets. It said the Army had wrongly relaxed the fuel efficiency standard. GAO denied the protest. No offeror had been able to meet the stricter standard. The relaxed one met the Army's needs and widened the field.

The firm's claim that it could now meet the old standard changed nothing. An agency need not keep a term that shuts out all rivals when a looser term serves its purpose.
gao-gaoreports-b-295529-4:
Johnson Controls World Services sought its protest costs in GAO file B-295529.4, dated August 19, 2005. The costs arose from the Walter Reed A-76 fight, over base operations support at the medical center. GAO granted the request. The first protest filing had clearly flagged flaws in the Army's cost judgment. The agency admitted it never probed those detailed claims. It also held back relevant papers for more than 70 days, until a hearing forced them out.

On those facts, the agency had let a clearly sound protest drag. The delay in corrective action, undue in GAO's word, is what opens the door to repayment.
gao-gaoreports-b-295582-4:
Dated October 5, 2005, GAO file B-295582.4 records Brewbaker White Sands JV as the protester. The Air Force had awarded NASCENT Group JV a contract for base engineering services at Holloman Air Force Base, New Mexico. The winner's offer was rated slightly lower but priced lower too. Past performance was the top factor, and the protester's rating there was slightly higher. GAO denied the protest. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release.

The selection official had weighed the offers in an integrated way. Both firms' past performance posed much the same risk, the official found. The premium for the protester's edge in rating was not worth paying.
gao-gaoreports-b-295952-4:
LENS, JV, sought its protest costs in GAO file B-295952.4, dated December 12, 2005. The Navy had run a utility privatization program at Marine Corps Base Hawaii, at Kaneohe Bay. The firm lost and protested the agency's should cost method for running the electric system. The agency then took corrective action. GAO denied the cost request. This copy is a redacted version cleared for release. Corrective action alone does not earn repayment of protest costs.

The protest must also be shown clearly meritorious on the record. That showing, GAO held, was not made here. The firm's challenge to the cost method stayed unproven.
gao-gaoreports-b-295990-4:
Cogent Systems protested an Army award for a fingerprint system for Iraq in GAO decision B-295990.4, dated October 6, 2005. The winner was Motorola. The system was an Automated Fingerprint Identification System. Cogent attacked the tech marks, the price review, and the final pick. Its low price bid had been ruled not fit for award.

GAO sustained the protest. A key flaw on a flatbed scanner was not well founded. GAO also found the agency gave no real talks on that point. With that flaw gone, the bar to award fell. Readers can use the case for how a weak flaw and thin talks can undo a pick.
gao-gaoreports-b-296090-4:
Kola Nut Travel again protested Army travel service awards in GAO decision B-296090.4, dated August 25, 2005. This time the winners were Alamo Travel Group and Wingate Travel. The firm said its tech bid was marked too low. It also said fee deals tied to the winners were improper.

GAO denied the protest. The review notes backed a mark of just acceptable for the firm's bid. On fees, GAO saw no proof of undue sway. The winners won on lower prices and higher marks. The case pairs with the firm's first protest. It shows the same fee claim fail on a fuller record.
gao-gaoreports-b-296194-4:
Foster-Miller protested its cut from the same Army CREW jammer contest in GAO decision B-296194.4, dated August 31, 2005. The system helps stop roadside bomb blasts. The firm was barred from field tests. It had sought to swap its program load for the field test.

GAO denied the protest. The test plans barred a new load after the first test round. GAO said that read of the plans was sound. The firm also failed to show its low mark on a key point was wrong. The cut from the field thus stood. The ruling shows test rules bind both sides once set.
gao-gaoreports-b-296435-4:
Port-A-Pit Catering protested its loss in the same Forest Service food contest in GAO decision B-296435.4, dated September 15, 2005. The work was hot and cold meals at 27 field sites. The firm hit how bids were scored. Price review was the core flaw it named. Other firms won at some sites.

GAO sustained the protest. The price review used unit prices alone. That base was too thin to match the true cost of rival bids. With no sound way to match costs, the call that prices were not fair fell. Price review must give a real base to match bids. Unit prices alone failed that test here.
gao-gaoreports-b-296628-4:
Ystueta protested the axing of an Agriculture call for build work in GAO decision B-296628.4, dated February 27, 2006. The site was a research center in Stoneville, Mississippi. The call had been set aside for small firms. That bar was then lifted and the call was axed. The firm said the acts dodged an award to it.

GAO denied the protest. Lack of funds is a clear cause to axe a call. An agency cannot award a deal past its funds. That cause needs just a sound base. The fund gap gave that base here. Claims of dodge did not beat the fund facts. The axing thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-296783-4:
ITT Federal Services sought protest costs after its win in the Europe logistics case in GAO decision B-296783.4, dated April 26, 2006. The Army fought sums for lawyers and a hired expert. GAO had backed the firm in the first fight. The winner there was Kellogg, Brown and Root. Rate caps were the core fight now.

GAO set the rates by law. A plea for a rate above the 150 dollar cap must use the broad price index for all goods. The index for legal work alone does not count. Pay for a hired expert was capped at the top federal pay rate. That cap held even when the expert billed more.
gao-gaoreports-b-297022-4:
Alion Science again protested the spectrum design award in GAO decision B-297022.4, dated September 26, 2006. The winner was again the ITT unit. The agency had done fix work after the first loss. It read the goods of the winner, its rivals, and its buyers. It weighed how the job could sway those stakes.

GAO denied this protest. The fix work met the flaw from the first case. Notes now showed a full clash check. The winner would use walled-off sub firms for clash parts of the work. That wall was judged fit to block the clash. Harm to work grade was small. A sound fix can cure a clash flaw.
gao-gaoreports-b-297053-4:
Haworth protested a General Services award for office furniture in GAO decision B-297053.4, dated June 7, 2006. The winner was Herman Miller. The site was a new federal block in San Francisco. All bid goods had to sit on the firm's schedule deal by a set date. The firm's quote was cut for a miss on that date.

GAO denied the protest. The agency had told firms of the date rule in clear terms. The firm failed to make sure all its goods were on the deal in time. That miss was its own. A fresh claim raised late in briefs was cut as late. Facts for it were known at the first filing.
gao-gaoreports-b-297534-4:
CHE Consulting protested the terms of a Defense call for gear upkeep in GAO decision B-297534.4, dated May 17, 2006. The gear was StorageTek kit at sites round the land. The call asked firms to show how they would get maker help. That help was a back-up if a fix failed in the set time. The firm said that term asked too much.

GAO denied the protest. The record gave a sound base for the term. The work was key upkeep with a tight fix clock. A back-up path to the maker is a fair need in that case. Terms that track a real risk can stand, even if they narrow the field.
gao-gaoreports-b-297790-4:
T Square Logistics sought protest costs in GAO decision B-297790.4, dated April 26, 2006. The first fight hit an Air Force award for base support. The site was Grissom Air Reserve Base in Indiana. The winner was Data Monitor Systems. Talks in the first case had flaws. The agency fixed the buy late, after a GAO talks track.

GAO backed pay of the costs. The claims were clearly strong, as the talks track showed. The agency was slow to fix the buy. Talks had cut the firm's past work mark to low trust for gaps in skill. That flaw drove the high price pick. Talks never named that gap to the firm.
gao-gaoreports-b-298033-4:
American Systems Consulting protested a Defense award in GAO decision B-298033.4, dated March 28, 2007. The winner was ManTech Security Technologies. The work was systems and software help. The user was the Defense Commissary Agency. The firm hit tech and cost marks. It also sought costs for past protests on this call.

GAO denied the protest and the cost plea. The record backed the agency finds on marks. The winner was higher rated on tech and lower on price. That mix is a strong win base. Past protest costs were not backed on this record. A firm that loses on marks and shows no cost base will get no costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-298099-4:
Overlook Systems again protested the GPS center award in GAO decision B-298099.4, dated November 28, 2006. The winner was again LinQuest. The agency had done a fresh clash check. It took a full plan to curb clash risk from the winner. It also added more watch steps of its own. The firm said the plan was too thin and talks were unfair.

GAO denied the protest. The clash risk was found to be not great. That find was sound on a deep check. The plan, as honed, plus more watch, was fit to guard the state. Talks on clash go to fitness to win. They need not be held with all firms. The pick thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298443-4:
Partnership for Response and Recovery protested corrective action by the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The case grew from a prior protest of awards for housing inspection services. Those services send inspectors to homes after a disaster. GAO ruled in B-298443.4 on December 18, 2006.

FEMA chose to reopen talks and seek fully revised proposals. The protester said that broad fix unfairly favored its rival. GAO disagreed. The agency had found its first talks and scoring weak. New needs had also been added to the work. An agency may widen a fix to match such flaws. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298489-4:
Compunetix, Inc. protested a NASA award to Frequentis USA, Inc. The Goddard Space Flight Center ran the buy. The contract covered Mission Operations Voice Enhancement systems. The work spans design, build, test, and upkeep of voice gear. GAO ruled in B-298489.4 and B-298489.5 on January 12, 2007.

Compunetix held a lower-rated, higher-priced proposal. It attacked nearly every step of the scoring. It also said the awardee was not a small firm fit for this set-aside. GAO reviewed the full record. It found the agency's calls fair and in line with the stated scheme. The broad attack did not hold up. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298575-4:
Alaska Structures, Inc. asked GAO to back payment of its protest costs. The plea grew from an Army buy for a mobile field hospital system. The Army Medical Research Acquisition Activity ran that buy. GAO acted in B-298575.4, a costs ruling, on January 22, 2007.

The agency had taken corrective action after the protest. It pledged to cancel and reissue the request. Cost payment turns on a protest being clearly sound. GAO found no such clear merit here. It also saw no proof for a linked claim from an earlier protest round. A weak protest earns no cost award. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-298833-4:
IBM Global Business Services protested an Air Force task order to Computer Sciences Corporation. The order named a system integrator for the Expeditionary Combat Support System. The work deploys shelf software and change management methods. GAO ruled in B-298833.4 and B-298833.5 on March 1, 2007.

The agency scored IBM's offer as high risk. Its plan used too few government staff in the change work. Key change tasks needed more agency hands than the plan gave. IBM's ratio of staff to consultants fell well below trade norms. That gap backed the risk mark. The terms attack also failed. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298918-4:
EBSCO Publishing, Inc. sought payment of its protest costs from the Department of Defense Education Activity. The agency had taken a fix after the firm's protest. That protest fought its removal from a buy for online information services. GAO acted in B-298918.4, a costs ruling, on May 7, 2007.

GAO backed payment of $20,945.95 in costs. It also took up the cap on lawyer fees. That cap sits at $150 per hour by statute. GAO urged that the cap be raised to match cost-of-living growth. The agency did not fight the raise or the sum claimed. The full claim could go forward.
gao-gaoreports-b-299145-4:
The Air Force sought a fresh look at a prior ruling in the combat search and rescue aircraft case. That ruling had backed protests by Sikorsky and Lockheed Martin Systems Integration-Owego. The award to The Boeing Company sat at the core. GAO acted in B-299145.4 on March 29, 2007.

The agency asked GAO to rule on points left open before. One point was a past performance mark for one protester. GAO found the mark of little confidence fair. Recent, badly flawed work on a like aircraft drove that mark. Strong work on a second like deal did not erase it. One grave lapse on close work can shape the score.
gao-gaoreports-b-299229-4:
MELE Associates, Inc. protested the rejection of its proposal by the Department of Energy. The buy sought services to find, remove, and guard nuclear and radiological materials. Those stocks sit at sites at risk of theft or misuse. GAO ruled in B-299229.4 on July 25, 2007.

The agency scored the bid under technical approach and firm experience. The bid pledged to meet the terms. But it did not show how it would do so. GAO found that gap showed a weak grasp of the work. The bid also failed to prove past work on like tasks. Thin claims in place of proof can sink a bid. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299260-4:
Swales Aerospace sought payment of its protest costs from NASA. The plea grew from protests of an award to SGT, Inc. That deal covered mechanical systems engineering services at Goddard Space Flight Center. GAO acted in B-299260.4, a costs ruling, on April 30, 2007.

Cost payment needs a strong protest plus slow agency action. The agency here had taken a fix in reply to the protests. GAO asked if that fix came with undue delay. It found no such delay on the record. Nor did the protests stand as clearly sound from the start. A plea built on those grounds fails. GAO denied the request.
gao-gaoreports-b-299307-4:
Panacea Consulting, Inc. protested Labor Department task orders to Systems Integration and Development, Inc. The orders covered project management support and core research support services. Both ran through a federal supply schedule deal. GAO ruled in B-299307.4 and B-299308.4 on July 27, 2007.

The record, GAO found, was too thin to back the award. Scores sat on the page with no real account of why. The pick memo likewise gave no sound logic. An agency must show the sense behind its marks. A bare score sheet leaves rivals and reviewers in the dark. Such a void cannot support a source selection. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299317-4:
The Department of the Army asked GAO to revisit its ruling in the Iraq linguist services case. That ruling had backed a protest by L-3 Communications Titan Corporation. The award to Global Linguist Solutions, LLC was at stake. GAO acted in B-299317.4 on June 8, 2007.

A fresh look needs more than a wish to reargue the case. GAO held to its prior call. The scoring flaws it found before stood on the record. The fill-rate and benchmark points had been weighed with care. The agency's plea gave no sound base to flip the result. GAO denied the reconsideration request. The prior ruling stayed in place.
gao-gaoreports-b-299582-4:
Korrect Optical protested a Veterans Affairs award to Safe-Lite Optical Company. The contract covered eyeglasses for veterans at medical centers in one network. The firm said the winner's bid missed a key term. GAO ruled in B-299582.4 and B-299582.5 on September 7, 2007.

The claimed gap was the count of frame styles on offer. The record showed the winner did meet that count. With that claim gone, the pick came down to price. The agency found the bids near equal on non-price points. A lower price can then break the tie. That path fit the best-value terms. No flaw in the firm's own score was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-299721-4:
The Mangi Environmental Group protested an Agriculture Department award to Geo Marine. The contract covered programmatic environmental assessments. The work grew from a settlement on haying and grazing lands in 20 states. GAO ruled in B-299721.4 on January 24, 2008.

The firm attacked the technical review and the pick. GAO found the agency's dim view of its bid fair. The bid read as muddled on key points. It held many flaws and gaps across its pages. A muddled bid gives a panel little to credit. The flaws were the firm's to cure at draft time. No breach of the stated tests was shown. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-310372-4:
Pemco Aeroplex, Inc. saw its protest thrown out. GAO ruled in B-310372.4 on May 2, 2008. The case ties to the Air Force KC-135 depot care race. Pemco claimed the Air Force's true needs had shifted in a big way. It said the call no longer matched those needs. It asked for a fresh race on new terms.

GAO dismissed the protest. The agency aide who turns needs into deal terms swore a key fact. The agency has made no call yet on shifts to the deal's terms. A claim built on a shift not yet made has no base. The race terms stand for now.
gao-gaoreports-b-310398-4:
Protest costs are backed in this GAO decision, B-310398.4, dated January 16, 2008. World Communications Center, Inc. had fought a sole-source award for satellite trackers. The Drug Enforcement Agency made that award to NAL Research Corporation. The firm said the agency shut it out of a fair test of its gear. It then asked for its protest costs back.

GAO backed the cost claim. The agency did not fight the claim at all. The file shows the agency was slow to fix a plain flaw. The first protests had clear merit on their face. Slow fixes to clear flaws can leave an agency owing protest costs.
gao-gaoreports-b-310489-4:
Superlative Technologies, Inc. won a fresh ruling (GAO decision B-310489.4, dated June 3, 2008). The case picks up a past fight on a Justice grants office buy. The office had killed its call for data safety help. It cited fears of leaks and unfair edge. It then gave the work with no race to a team that held a firm tied to the leaks.

GAO held the acts cannot be squared. The kill rests on fears the next act mocks. The office wrote down no facts on what was shared or with whom. If a buy restarts on a new path, set steps to clear taint claims must be heeded.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-4:
People hurt while protecting the public get very different disability pay. Report GAO-06-4, issued April 7, 2006, compares benefits for military personnel and civilian public safety officers. Congress ordered the study. It covers federal staff and staff in six states and six cities. The local focus is on firefighters. The state focus is on state police.

GAO listed benefits for temporary disability. It did the same for permanent partial and permanent total disability. It then figured the lifetime present value for sample people in varied cases. Amounts change with program rules and personal facts. Readers get a rare side-by-side view of unlike systems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-4: GAO's 2007 report looks at pay for Cold War bomb-plant workers sickened by rays and poisons on the job. It urges tighter watch over the payout contractors, a clearer public view of Labor's role, and a truly free hand for the board that judges claims. The heart of it: sick workers deserve a fair shake, not a stacked deck.
gargantua-and-pantagruel-illustrated-boo:
Book 4 of Rabelais's five-book work, Englished by Peter Antony Motteux, puts Pantagruel and Panurge to sea. They sail in search of the Oracle of the Bottle, which Panurge hopes will settle whether he should wed. A translator's preface warns readers that the author shows little soft good nature, and much bold sport.

The voyage hops from island to island, each stranger than the last. The crew meets odd peoples, strange foods, fierce storms, and lands where words freeze in the air. Talk at table turns to souls, fate, and old tales of how long life lasts. The sea trip lets Rabelais mix sailor's yarn, learned debate, and gross fun in one long, loose chain of scenes.
gerfaut-volume-4:
Dinner at the Bergenheim table fills Gerfaut, Volume 4, the closing English portion of Charles de Bernard's French novel of 1838. The Baron's gaiety sounds forced beside his wife's quiet sadness, and the company senses weather it cannot name. Octave de Gerfaut, the guest whose fame won him his chair, sits inside the secret that is breaking the house. Bernard lets small talk carry the pressure the principals dare not speak.

Inside, the attachment between guest and baroness moves past the point where silence can protect it. The Baron's suffering, hidden under boisterous manners, breaks through in scenes of strained hospitality. Lambernier, the dismissed workman nursing his own revenge, waits at the design's edge like a second fate. Bernard drives the country-house tragedy to exposure and its bitter settlements. Readers finishing Gerfaut get the payoff of the slow build: manners and desire colliding in a house where everyone performs happiness.
germany-from-the-earliest-period-volume-:
Wolfgang Menzel's history of Germany, Englished by Mrs. George Horrocks from the fourth German edition, reaches its last volume here. A supplementary chapter by Edgar Saltus brings events nearer to the reader's own day. The volume opens with the rise of Prussia and moves through art, courts, and wars. Its middle is given to the great struggle with France.

Pages here weigh Napoleon's plans in 1870: armies massed at Metz and Strasburg, and supply services in hopeless confusion. Day by day, the French lose the time they need, while German forces close in. Menzel writes as a German patriot of the old school, in long, rich chapters. The volume closes a vast survey that runs from the earliest tribes to a united empire.
godolphin-volume-4:
Volume 4 of Godolphin opens at chapter thirty-two, on the weakness of virtue that springs only from feeling. Godolphin is in Rome, on the eve of departure. A mantled figure that recalls Lucilla slips past in the dark before he can be sure. At his rooms he searches his papers in vain, then sits in moody thought over a long, kind letter he wrote her the day before.

In that letter he laid bare his struggles and his self-sacrifice, as far as one of her simple experience could grasp them. He hides nothing of his love, yet holds to his course. The Roman chapters give the novel its most inward turn. Lytton slows the plot to dwell on conscience, memory, and a love that duty has fenced off.
govdocs-archive_org-ufo4_20240815_UFO_de: UFO made public docs 4: the made public government document, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, filed. From the archive shelves, for readers of the files and readers and readers.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's fourth volume, with Milman's notes, opens at chapter thirty-nine with Theodoric the Ostrogoth, his conquest of Italy, and the Gothic kingdom he built there. Boethius, the senator-philosopher Theodoric executed, closes that chapter's survey. Chapter forty then begins the reign of Justinian, with the Empress Theodora and the circus factions.

The volume covers Justinian's codification of Roman law, Belisarius's reconquests, the wars with Persia, and the empire's state under his successors, ending near chapter forty-eight. Gibbon's legal chapters pause over Papinian, the Theodosian code, and the rescripts. Byzantium here reaches its last great expansion, already showing the strains Gibbon blames for later decline.
humboldt-cosmos-otte-vol-4:
Volume four of Humboldt's Cosmos, in Otté's translation, comes down from the stars to the Earth itself. The Bohn edition of 1849 carried the set to English readers. Humboldt treats our planet as one body: its figure, density, inner heat, and magnetic currents.

Volcanoes and earthquakes get long, careful treatment, drawn from his years in the Andes and Mexico. He maps how magnetic force varies over the globe, work his own expeditions had driven. The volume is geology and geophysics before those sciences had settled names. Humboldt's web of observing stations, built to feed such a book, helped found the modern earth sciences.
humboldt-personal-narrative-williams-vol:
Volume four of Humboldt's Personal Narrative, in Helen Maria Williams's translation, appeared in 1819. The expedition turns from the Orinoco toward Cuba and then to the high Andes. Humboldt's pen keeps its double register: barometer readings beside sweeping views of nature.

The party revisits the coast, crosses to Havana, and returns to sail for Cartagena and the Magdalena river. Ahead lie Bogota's high plain and the climb into the Andes proper. Humboldt studies the politics and products of the Spanish colonies as keenly as their volcanoes. The volume shows his science widening into a study of whole societies and their lands.
ihne-history-rome-vol-4:
Reform and ruin mark the fourth volume of Ihne's History of Rome, from 1871. The Gracchi brothers seek land and justice for the poor. Marius and Sulla then march legions against Rome itself, and the free state begins its slow unmaking.

Ihne brings a modern eye for deep causes to the collapse. Wealth, empire, and faction rot the constitution from within, in his view. The revolution, he shows, was one nobody planned and nobody could stop. His volume teaches how a republic can die by inches, a lesson that gave his Roman history a grave, lasting relevance for modern readers.
isbe-1915-vol-4:
The fourth volume of the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia appeared in 1915, bringing Orr's great project near the alphabet's end. Five volumes were planned, and the fourth shows no slackening of the plan. The vast survey of Bible lands and teachings draws toward its close.

Entries continue through the later letters, with the same mix of archaeology, history, languages, and doctrine that marks the set. Orr's team kept its thorough standard to the last article, answering the questions students actually brought to the text. The encyclopedia became the reference shelf's cornerstone for a generation of pastors and teachers. Volume 4 leaves the work all but complete, awaiting only the final volume and its indexes. It remains a fair sample of the set's quality at full stretch.
j-s-le-fanu-s-ghostly-tales-volume-4:
Joseph Sheridan Le Fanu's Ghostly Tales, volume four, gathers Chapelizod stories of 1851 and earlier pieces of 1838 and 1850. The Drunkard's Dream, The Ghost and the Bone-setter, and The Mysterious Lodger are named. Chapelizod opens with a joke that every ancient village has its legends of terror. A decayed cheese without mites is as unlikely, he says.

The Mysterious Lodger turns on an advertisement in the Times. A couple in debt let a room to clear what they owe in three insertions. Economy per line shapes their tempting wording. Village ghosts and Dublin lodgings share this fourth volume.
jataka-cowell-vol-4:
Volume four of the Jataka in Cowell's edition appeared in 1901, with W. H. D. Rouse chief among its translators from the Pali. The six-volume set was the first complete English Jataka. By this volume the tales have grown longer and more courtly.

The Bodhisatta is born in high stations here: minister, prince, and wise judge at royal courts. The stories turn on statecraft, law, and the testing of character under power. Verses still anchor each tale, some of them among the oldest lines in the canon. Cowell's team kept the flavor of the Pali storytelling. The volume shows the Jataka at full stretch, halfway to its end.
jefferson-writings-vol-4:
Volume Four of Jefferson's writings gathers his letters and papers from the 1790s. Jefferson spent that decade as secretary of state, then in opposition, then as vice president. The 1903 Lipscomb and Bergh edition orders the record year by year.

The French Revolution, the fight over a national bank, and the rise of parties fill these pages. Jefferson argues for strict limits on federal power and for friendship with France. His private letters are often blunter than his public acts. The volume is key evidence for how the first American party wars began. Letters to Madison and Monroe show the opposition planning its moves.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-4:
Aaron, elder brother of Moses, is the subject of this long Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He was the elder son of Amram and Jochebed of the tribe of Levi, the entry states, with Moses three years younger and Miriam older. While Moses was raised at the Egyptian court, Aaron stayed with his kin. His eloquent speech made him Moses' spokesman to Israel and to Pharaoh.

Aaron shared the signs and the first plagues, stretching out his rod at Moses' command. Rabbinic tradition makes him a peacemaker who reconciled husbands, wives, and neighbors. The whole house of Israel wept at his death. His part in the Golden Calf is told against him as well.
joshua-volume-4:
Volume four of Georg Ebers's Joshua opens at chapter twenty, in a storm over the isthmus. Waves dash in the lakes, and the Red Sea is lashed to fury. Pharaoh's army camps below the Migdol of the South, its tents straining at their pins. Fires ringed by double rows of soldiers fight the gale through the night.

Three hours after sunset, a slender youth approaches the northern gate guards. His thick black locks are tangled and his feet covered with dust and dried clay. Yet his bearing is a freeman's, and his messenger's pass is perfectly correct. He asks the way to Prince Siptah's tent. This volume carries the Exodus story toward Pharaoh's pursuit and ruin.
journeys-through-bookland-vol-4:
Volume four of Journeys Through Bookland gathers poems and stories for young readers under Charles H. Sylvester's reading plan. Longfellow stands large in the contents: Footsteps of Angels, The Village Blacksmith, and The Wreck of the Hesperus. A sketch of Longfellow's life and Lowell's poem to him appear as well.

Whittier's Barefoot Boy, Wordsworth's My Heart Leaps Up, and Tennyson's Song of the Brook add more verse. A Dog of Flanders, by Louise de la Ramée, gives the volume a long story. Father Ryan, Coates Kinney, Goldsmith, and the Cary sisters all contribute. Sylvester built each volume to train taste by pleasure. This one leans toward American poetry and song.
lecky-england-18th-vol-4:
America rebels in the fourth volume of Lecky's History, in the 1892 printing. Taxes, defiance, and war cost Britain her thirteen colonies at last. Lecky, an Irish liberal, judges the quarrel with rare fairness toward both sides of the Atlantic.

He grants the colonists their grievances and the ministers their dilemmas alike. Few British historians of his age treated the Revolution so evenly. The empire's greatest failure gets a cool head and a full hearing here. Readers meet a model of how to write a foe's history with honor, in a volume long prized for its balance and breadth.
littre-dictionary-1863-vol-4:
The fourth volume finished Littré's Dictionary of the French Language, completing a work that had occupied its author for decades. Littré published the first volume in 1863; the set closed with the alphabet's end and the supplements he added. Few dictionaries in any language have been so much one man's monument.

Volume 4 carries the entries to Z, every word given its history and its reasons, in Littré's phrase. The French language stands recorded from A to Z with a fullness no tongue had received before. Four volumes remain the model of what a historical dictionary can achieve, the standard against which the Academy's own work is judged. The monument stands whole: the French tongue's complete biography, written by the scholar who devoted his life to it.
lord-ormont-and-his-aminta-volume-4:
Volume 4 of George Meredith's novel takes up Book 4, beginning with Lady Charlotte's triumph. Lady Charlotte returns to the country around Steignton, where she was born and bred. A bright day over park, lake, and river frames her ride with Weyburn.

Later chapters follow pursuers on the road back and a scene at the Jolly Cricketers inn. The Ormont jewels enter the story as brother and sister begin their contention. Undercurrents run through the minds of both Lady Charlotte and Lord Ormont. Meredith keeps pride, family honor, and love in close combat. The volume drives the marriage crisis toward its breaking point.
lucian-works-fowler-vol-4:
Volume four closes the Fowler brothers' complete Lucian of 1905. The final gathering completes the works of antiquity's great skeptic in English. His send-ups of superstition and religious hucksters stand out in this volume.

Lucian exposes miracle-mongers and fraudulent prophets with obvious delight. He also writes literary criticism, mock encomiums, and dialogues of the dead. The range shows why Renaissance humanists treasured him as a model. Two thousand years on, many of his targets still walk among us. The Fowlers' translation served English readers as the standard Lucian for decades. Ending the set, this volume completes a remarkable act of translation.
madame-chrysantheme-volume-4:
Volume 4 closes Pierre Loti's Madame Chrysanthème, as Gutenberg etext 81. The four volumes together form his famous Japanese diary-novel. Loti wrote it from his own summer as a naval officer at Nagasaki. His temporary marriage there gives the book its bittersweet frame.

The season ends, as such seasons must, with departure. Chrysanthème is left behind as the ship takes her officer away. Loti's diary style keeps every scene fresh and immediate. Europe read the book as a window on old Japan. Its mix of beauty, irony, and sadness still holds readers. This last volume completes one of France's best-known travel tales.
melmoth-the-wanderer-vol-1-of-4:
Charles Robert Maturin published Melmoth the Wanderer in 1820. Archibald Constable printed it in Edinburgh, in four volumes. Maturin was known then as the author of the play Bertram.

Volume one opens the tale, as its title page states plainly. He gave the romance to the Marchioness of Abercorn. A copy note says great care was taken to match the first printing. Old spellings and odd marks stand as they were first set in type. Hurst, Robinson and Company sold the book in London as well. The set's age and fame rest much on this first part.
memoirs-of-madame-la-marquise-de-montesp:
Book four of Madame de Montespan's memoirs opens at chapter forty nine. President de Nesmond stands at the head of that chapter. A tame husband and his love sick wife make its sad tale.

Montespan says Nesmond served her well in her suits at law. He wed late, at sixty five, a farmer's daughter named Clorinde. She soon gave her heart to a young Spaniard at a dance. Her frank words to her husband show no shame at all in the act. A sad sequel is promised in the chapter heads. Court love tales here end in grief more often than joy.
merivale-romans-empire-vol-4:
Decline stalks the fourth volume of Merivale's History, from 1865. Commodus, the gladiator emperor, shames the throne he inherits from a philosopher father. The Severan house follows, then the third century dissolves into anarchy, plague, and rival emperors in every province.

Merivale closes his main narrative with the Empire's long afternoon. Glory fades into civil war as the frontiers crack under strain. He tells the sunset of Rome without flinching and without despair. The volume earns its somber power honestly, tracing how a world state can rot at the center while its forms still stand grand and hollow.
miscellaneous-writings-and-speeches-volu:
Volume Four of Macaulay's works contains his parliamentary speeches, dedicated to the Marquess of Lansdowne. Macaulay's preface admits he publishes them most reluctantly. He suspended his historical work, he says, to prepare the speeches, and fears reviving old party passions. Expressions applauded in fierce times may now seem intemperate, he warns.

He writes with special pain about his encounters with Sir Robert Peel. Yet he praises Peel's later moderation, sacrifices, and great services, and records their reconciliation. Macaulay insists his hostility was political, never personal. The speeches preserve a leading Whig orator reviewing his own career with unusual candor.
motley-united-netherlands-vol-4:
Maurice of Nassau wins the fourth volume of Motley's United Netherlands, from 1869. His brilliant campaigns push Spain back town by town and field by field. The road runs toward the Twelve Years' Truce, which seals the Republic's survival in law as his sword sealed it in fact.

Motley closes his great history as the Dutch golden age dawns. Ships, painters, and scholars reward eighty years of war in his ending. The young captain's genius anchors the tale's final triumph. Readers leave with a full epic of a free state's birth, told by an American who made Holland's struggle a classic of English prose.
my-mother-s-rival-everyday-life-library-:
Charlotte M. Brame, who also wrote Dora Thorne, tells this tale of a mother's rival. It ran as number four in the Everyday Life Library. The book opens with hard questions about criminals' children. What becomes of the sons and daughters of hanged men?

The narrator recalls a gentleman lately tried and executed for murder. His fair-haired little son knew nothing of the crime. Does the boy hear his father's name as he grows? Would a suitor be told he courts a murderer's child? Brame builds her tale on that hidden shame, in the lush, feeling style that made her dime novels sell.
nasa-tm-19690029614-comparison-of-coinci:
J. M. Grebowsky, N. K. Rahman, and M. A. Taylor compare coincident OGO 3 and OGO 4 ion composition measurements in this June 1969 Goddard preprint, X-621-69-263. OGO 4 orbited over the poles through the topside ionosphere. OGO 3 flew a stretched magnetospheric orbit, and the two craft sometimes sampled the same region at the same time.

Measurements from two August 1967 nightside passes through the plasmasphere anchor the comparison. Chapters first compare ion densities in general terms across most midlatitude regions. Local time effects on the agreement are examined next. A section on diffusion coupling follows, since linked ion flows can shift both instruments' readings. Conclusions and a bibliography close the cross-check between the two observatories.
nasa-tm-19710018262-vehicle-attitude-an-:
Vehicle Attitude, an Analysis of Flight 4.272 UA, is a NASA report on one sounding rocket flight. It reconstructs which way the rocket pointed during flight, a fact researchers need before they can interpret its instruments' readings. The determination rests on two kinds of sensors carried aboard the vehicle.

Solar aspect sensors read the Sun's direction, while magnetometers read Earth's magnetic field, and together they fix the attitude. The report walks through data acquisition, the sensors themselves, and the computer program used to reduce the raw data. It explains the tabulated results and the vehicle's actual motion. The authors present it as a brief case history of the method, useful for later rocket flights.
nex-pelle-the-conqueror-vol-4:
Nexo brings his four-volume epic to a close in the final English volume of Pelle the Conqueror. The heat of early struggle cools into the long work of building and compromise. Pelle, now older and wiser, takes the long view of what the fights have won.

Victory here is partial, as it is in real life. The movement matures, and so does its hero, with scars to show for both. Nexo ends not with a trumpet blast but with hard-earned wisdom. The full set stands as Denmark's great novel of labor and hope.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-1-vol-4:
Volume four of Schaff's Nicene Fathers, first series, holds Augustine's writings against two great foes: the Manichaeans and the Donatists. The volume came out in 1886. Augustine had belonged to the Manichaean sect for nine years before he broke with it, which sharpens these pages.

Against the Manichaeans, he defends the goodness of creation and the free will that alone makes evil. Against the Donatists, a rival African church born in persecution, he argues the true church is marked by unity and love, not by the purity of its ministers. The fights look ancient; the questions, on evil and on schism, are not. The volume is Augustine the controversialist.
nicene-post-nicene-fathers-2-vol-4:
Athanasius of Alexandria fills volume four of the Nicene Fathers' second series, from 1890: select works and letters. Athanasius spent his long bishopric fighting the Arian teaching that Christ was a created being. Five emperors exiled him five times; he died in office in 373.

His On the Incarnation, written young, states the classic case: God became man so man might become godlike. The orations against the Arians then argue Christ's full divinity from scripture. His festal letters fix the date of Easter and list the books of the New Testament as we still have them. The volume is the Nicene faith's own arsenal.
night-and-morning-volume-4:
Volume four of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Night and Morning holds Book the Fourth of the novel. A line from Wilson's City of the Plague heads the first chapter, about a sweet gleam of sunshine on a lake. Lytton then turns to a drop of water under a solar microscope.

Monsters in that drop, he says, can make a drinker loathe pure water for a day. Yet thirst soon makes him forget the horrid unseen life within. So it is with Life itself, Lytton argues. Folks loll in sleek comfort until some ghastly corner of the world is shown to them. The image frames the darker turns of this book.
northern-lights-volume-4:
Volume four of Gilbert Parker's Northern Lights holds four tales, opening with A Man, a Famine, and a Heathen Boy. The Healing Springs and the Pioneers follows it. The Little Widow of Jansen and Watching the Rise of Orion close the volume. All four sit in Canada's far country.

The first tale sets its scene in Athabasca, in the Far North. Parker calls it one of the most beautiful countries in summer. Winter there is cold and bare, though Chinook winds from the Pacific soften the Rockies' fierceness. He explains a poudre day, when powdered frost hangs shining in the air. That powder, he warns, bites skin white in short order.
one-of-our-conquerors-volume-4:
George Meredith's fourth volume opens with book four. Chapter twenty-five shows Nataly in action in London. Visitors bring rumors of singers and news of Skepsey. Miss Radnor, called Nesta, draws warm praise from guests. A grand basso reports that she is well.

Later chapters treat Mrs. Marsett and a virgin's shadows. Nesta carries a burden as secrets press closer. Squires must conquer themselves in a conqueror's service. A pair of wooers and kindled tempers follow on. Meredith writes brilliant, crowded scenes of society talk. The volume moves the family toward its crisis.
orderic-vitalis-ecclesiastical-history-f:
The fourth volume of Thomas Forester's Orderic Vitalis, from 1856, completes the English set. Orderic's Ecclesiastical History ends in the early 1140s, in the wreck of King Stephen's reign. The old monk lays down his pen with a note on his own age and failing sight.

Anarchy in England, wars in Normandy, and the doings of bishops and abbots fill the last books. Orderic's eye for character never dims: he gives motives, speeches, and second thoughts. The chronicle he leaves is the fullest Norman record of the twelfth century. Forester's four volumes made this great monk readable in English for the first time.
pahlavi-texts-west-vol-4:
West's fourth volume of Pahlavi Texts appeared in 1892 as Sacred Books volume thirty-seven. Its subject is the contents of the Nasks, the lost holy books. The Nasks were the twenty-one books of Sasanian Persia's Avesta.

Most of those books no longer exist in complete form. Medieval priests had written summaries of each missing book's contents. West translated those summaries, preserving a map of a lost library. The volume reads half as index, half as grave-marker for burnt scriptures. Scholars use it to reconstruct what the full Avesta once held. Without such summaries, even the titles of most Nasks would be unknown.
palfrey-history-new-england-vol-4:
Volume 4 of Palfrey's history, from 1858, brings the great climax of his tale. The later seventeenth century shakes New England to its base. King Philip's War nearly wipes the young colonies off the map.

Governor Andros then tramples the old charters from his seat in Boston. Colonists resist, arrest him, and cheer the Glorious Revolution in England. Palfrey tells the drama with a patriot's warmth and a scholar's care. The Puritan order cracks, and a new age pushes through the breaks. Readers feel the old world ending across these stirring pages of revolt. Palfrey keeps sympathy for both crown and colony in balance.
pausanias-description-greece-frazer-vol-:
Volume four of Frazer's Pausanias covers central Greece and the islands in commentary. Delphi's oracle and Thebes' tragic past anchor the central Greek books. Aegean shrines and island cults extend the traveler's range here.

Frazer brings the full tools of classical archaeology to each passage. Coins, inscriptions, and excavation results all test Pausanias's statements. The ancient guidebook meets modern science, and both come out richer. Frazer, later famous for The Golden Bough, shows his comparative method developing. Readers can follow whole regions site by site with confidence. The volume proves how much history one careful traveler preserved almost by accident.
pentagon-papers-vol-4:
Volume 4 closes the Senator Gravel edition of the Pentagon Papers, the secret Vietnam history leaked in 1971. The study had been ordered by Defense Secretary Robert McNamara, who wanted a full record of how the United States slid into a major war. Its authors worked from the government's own files, which gave the leak its force.

The final volume covers the war's last years in the study, through the Tet Offensive and the first moves toward negotiation. It completes the record of decision-making from 1945 to 1968 across four volumes. The papers revealed years of private doubt hidden behind public confidence. Their release helped turn opinion against the war and remains the classic case of a whistleblower changing history.
personal-memoirs-of-p-h-sheridan-volume-:
Part 4 of volume 2 opens Sheridan's Shenandoah Valley campaign of 1864. Dissatisfied with intelligence from deserters and doubtful citizens, he builds a scout battalion from his own volunteer soldiers. Major H. K. Young commands them, and they ride in Confederate uniforms, paid from the Secret Service fund.

Through an old man selling vegetables into Winchester, Sheridan opens a channel to the loyal schoolteacher Rebecca Wright. Her information helps him decide to strike at Newtown. The chapter runs on to the battle of the Opequon, a turning movement, a cavalry charge, and victory.
personal-memoirs-of-u-s-grant-part-4: In the hosted sample, only the front matter of Part 4 of Grant's Personal Memoirs, the contents of volume 2, with no chapter text visible. The contents open at Chattanooga, with the battles of Wauhatchie, Lookout Mountain, and Missionary Ridge, then move to Grant's commission as lieutenant-general. Then come his first interview with President Lincoln and the planning of the grand campaign of 1864. Sherman's Georgia campaign, the crossing of the Rapidan, and the battle of the Wilderness follow.
pierre-and-his-people-tales-of-the-far-n:
Four tales make up Volume 4 of Gilbert Parker's Pierre and His People: The Tall Master, The Crimson Flag, and The Flood in Pipi Valley among them. The stories belong to his far north cycle, told among Indians, half-breeds, and men of the Hudson's Bay Company.

The Tall Master begins by admitting the story has been tossed about in so many mouths that travelers now hear only a doubtful version. Pretty Pierre, who was at Fort Luke when the battle occurred, sifted the facts, and the tale concerns a master said to dwell among strange tribes of the Far-Off Metal River. Their legends tell of a White Valley and Hills of the Mighty Men, and of a pleasant land lying toward the Arctic.
plato-dialogues-jowett-vol-4:
The fourth volume of Plato in Benjamin Jowett's translation gathers five late, hard dialogues. Parmenides lets the old philosopher Parmenides cross-examine a young Socrates and press hard on Plato's own theory of forms. Theaetetus asks what knowledge is, and ends without an answer.

Sophist and Statesman hunt for definitions: what marks a sophist, and what marks a true ruler. Philebus closes the volume by weighing pleasure against wisdom in the good life. These are Plato's most technical works, where the drama thins and the logic thickens. Scholars prize them for showing Plato testing his own system to its limits.
plutarch-s-lives-volume-1-of-4:
Plutarch's Lives, Volume One of Four, presents the Greek writer Plutarch in English translation by Aubrey Stewart and George Long. The edition was published in London by George Bell and Sons in eighteen ninety-four, with notes and a life of Plutarch included. Its preface calls Plutarch a favorite author since the revival of classical learning in Europe.

The Lives pair short biographies of Greek and Roman leaders, judging character through deeds, faults, and virtues. The preface argues that Plutarch makes ancient names feel like living people, gossiping pleasantly while instructing solidly. For many educated readers, it says, these lives were their main path into the ancient world. This volume opens the four-volume set.
plutarch-s-lives-volume-2-of-4:
Volume Two of Four of Plutarch's Lives continues the English translation by Aubrey Stewart and George Long, published in London by George Bell and Sons in eighteen ninety-nine. Plutarch, the Greek biographer, wrote paired lives of Greek and Roman figures, followed by a comparison of the pair. The contents list shows that pattern clearly throughout this volume.

Pairs here include Pelopidas with Marcellus, Aristeides with Marcus Cato, and Philopoemen with Titus Flamininus. Single lives cover Pyrrhus, Caius Marius, Lysander, Sulla, Kimon, and Lucullus, several of them translated by Long. Readers get character studies of generals and statesmen of Greece and Rome, weighed side by side for virtue, fortune, and fault, in Plutarch's moral, story-rich manner.
plutarch-s-lives-volume-3-of-4:
Volume Three of Four of Plutarch's Lives, in the English translation by Aubrey Stewart and the late George Long, was published in London by George Bell and Sons in eighteen ninety-two. Plutarch's paired biographies of Greek and Roman leaders are among the most read works of ancient history writing. The contents page maps this volume's pairs and comparisons.

Lives here cover Nikias, Crassus, Sertorius, Eumenes, Agesilaus, and Pompeius, each Greek or Roman pair followed by a comparison. The volume then gives lives of Alexander, Julius Caesar, Phokion, and Cato. Long translated several of the Roman lives. Together they trace ambition, generalship, and downfall across the classical world.
podcast-dannyjones-sG5I9Zc5p-4:
Author Ralph Blumenthal joins Danny Jones to tell the story of the Harvard psychiatrist who grew obsessed with alien abduction. The doctor was John Mack, a Harvard professor who took abduction reports at face value. Blumenthal wrote a book on Mack's life and work.

Blumenthal tells how Mack moved from a fine career in mind care to the fringe of UFO lore. He shares the cases that hooked Mack and the storm they caused at Harvard. Jones asks what made a top mind risk his name for such tales. Listeners get a sharp life story of faith in the face of scorn.
podcast-joerogan-sGFFPJDzN-4:
Aubrey Marcus joins Joe Rogan for episode 367, an early talk from before Marcus built his Onnit fitness brand into an empire. At the time he was a young voice for training both body and mind. The young show gave his ideas a long, open hearing.

Marcus talks through his approach to strength, focus, and a well-run life. He and Rogan share notes on training, diet, and the mental side of performance. The chat also touches psychedelics and self-testing, themes Marcus later built books and brands on. Listeners can hear the raw ideas before the business polish arrived.
quintilian-institutio-butler-loeb-vol-4:
Books nine through twelve close Quintilian's Institutio Oratoria in this fourth Loeb volume, translated by H. E. Butler. The twelve-book course ends where it aimed from the start: at the finished orator, trained in art and bound to be a good man. These last books are the most read of the set.

Figures of speech, memory systems, and delivery fill the first of them. Then Quintilian sketches the orator's whole life: his reading, his character, his duty to the state, and his rest in old age. His claim that only a good man can truly speak well became famous. The volume completes rhetoric's bible.
ranke-history-england-vol-4:
Elizabeth's middle years occupy Volume 4 of Ranke's History of England. The 1875 translation by Oxenford carries the tale toward open war. The long duel with Spain builds as the Armada draws near.

Ranke sets England inside the grand play of European statecraft. Sea power grows, plots thicken, and Mary of Scots meets her fate. The small island kingdom takes its place among the mighty states. Ranke writes at his most sweeping in this crowded volume. He links court moves in London to camps and fleets abroad. England's rise feels both fragile and fated under his steady gaze.
reymont-the-peasants-vol-4:
Summer brings Reymont's epic full circle in the fourth and final English volume of The Peasants. Harvest crowns the year's labor, and each soul in the village meets reward or reckoning. The Boryna family's long drama reaches its close under the hot sun.
